Medium 368. Largest Divisible Subset Google Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Return a largest subset where every pair (a, b) satisfies a % b == 0 or b % a == 0.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3]
Output: [1,2]
Explanation: [1,3] is also accepted.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,4,8]
Output: [1,2,4,8]

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 1000 · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 2 * 10⁹ · All the integers in nums are unique.

Hint 1

Sort the numbers. What structure must a divisible subset have?

Hint 2

It's a chain where each element divides the next: use an LIS-style DP.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying all subsets is O(2ⁿ · n²). The chain DP is O(n²).

Spot it: After sorting, a divisible subset is a chain where each element divides the next (divisibility is transitive). That's Longest Increasing Subsequence with nums[i] % nums[j] == 0 as the link.

Why not another pattern? Checking all subsets is O(2ⁿ).

Approach:

  1. Sort. size[i] = longest chain ending at i; parent[i] = previous element.
  2. For each j < i with nums[i] % nums[j] == 0: extend if size[j] + 1 is bigger.
  3. Rebuild from the index with the largest size.
class Solution:
    def largestDivisibleSubset(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        nums = sorted(nums)
        n = len(nums)
        size = [1] * n  # longest divisible chain ending at i
        parent = [-1] * n
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i):
                if nums[i] % nums[j] == 0 and size[j] + 1 > size[i]:
                    size[i] = size[j] + 1  # nums[j] divides nums[i]: extend its chain
                    parent[i] = j
        i = max(range(n), key=lambda t: size[t])
        subset = []
        while i != -1:
            subset.append(nums[i])  # walk the chain backwards
            i = parent[i]
        return subset[::-1]
function largestDivisibleSubset(nums: number[]): number[] {
    nums = [...nums].sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const n = nums.length;
    const size: number[] = new Array(n).fill(1);  // longest divisible chain ending at i
    const parent: number[] = new Array(n).fill(-1);
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (let j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (nums[i] % nums[j] === 0 && size[j] + 1 > size[i]) {
                size[i] = size[j] + 1;  // nums[j] divides nums[i]: extend its chain
                parent[i] = j;
            }
        }
    }
    let i = 0;
    for (let t = 1; t < n; t++) {
        if (size[t] > size[i]) {
            i = t;  // the first index with the longest chain
        }
    }
    const subset: number[] = [];
    while (i !== -1) {
        subset.push(nums[i]);  // walk the chain backwards
        i = parent[i];
    }
    return subset.reverse();
}
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> largestDivisibleSubset(int[] nums) {
        nums = nums.clone();
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] size = new int[n];  // longest divisible chain ending at i
        Arrays.fill(size, 1);
        int[] parent = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(parent, -1);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
                if (nums[i] % nums[j] == 0 && size[j] + 1 > size[i]) {
                    size[i] = size[j] + 1;  // nums[j] divides nums[i]: extend its chain
                    parent[i] = j;
                }
            }
        }
        int i = 0;
        for (int t = 1; t < n; t++) {
            if (size[t] > size[i]) {
                i = t;  // the first index with the longest chain
            }
        }
        List<Integer> subset = new ArrayList<>();
        while (i != -1) {
            subset.add(nums[i]);  // walk the chain backwards
            i = parent[i];
        }
        Collections.reverse(subset);
        return subset;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If a | b and b | c then a | c, so checking only consecutive chain elements is enough.
  2. This is the O(n²) LIS DP with a different link condition.
  3. Parent pointers rebuild one optimal chain.

  • Several answers of the same size (any is accepted).
  • 1 divides everything.

Complexity: O(n²) time, O(n) space.

Medium 377. Combination Sum IV Google Amazon Array

Problem: Count ordered sequences of numbers from nums (reusable) that add up to target.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3], target = 4
Output: 7
Explanation: The possible combination ways are: (1, 1, 1, 1) (1, 1, 2) (1, 2, 1) (1, 3) (2, 1, 1) (2, 2) (3, 1) Note that different sequences are counted as different combinations.
Example 2
Input: nums = [9], target = 3
Output: 0

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 200 · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 1000 · All the elements of nums are unique. · 1 ≤ target ≤ 1000

Hint 1

The last number of a sequence summing to t can be any x in nums.

Hint 2

Compare with Coin Change II: why does the loop order matter?

From brute force to the pattern: Listing every sequence is exponential. The DP is O(target · n).

Spot it: Sequences, not sets: different orders count separately. The last number of the sequence is any x, leaving t − x → 1D DP over the total with the target in the outer loop.

Why not another pattern? Coin Change II's loop order (coins outside) counts combinations, not sequences.

Approach:

  1. ways[0] = 1.
  2. For t from 1 to target: ways[t] = Σ ways[t − x] over x ≤ t.
class Solution:
    def combinationSum4(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        ways = [0] * (target + 1)
        ways[0] = 1  # the empty sequence
        for t in range(1, target + 1):  # totals outside: every order is counted
            for x in nums:
                if x <= t:
                    ways[t] += ways[t - x]  # sequences ending with x
        return ways[target]
function combinationSum4(nums: number[], target: number): number {
    const ways: number[] = new Array(target + 1).fill(0);
    ways[0] = 1;  // the empty sequence
    for (let t = 1; t <= target; t++) {  // totals outside: every order is counted
        for (const x of nums) {
            if (x <= t) {
                ways[t] += ways[t - x];  // sequences ending with x
            }
        }
    }
    return ways[target];
}
class Solution {
    public int combinationSum4(int[] nums, int target) {
        // long: totals we never need can grow past 2^31 even when the answer fits in an int
        long[] ways = new long[target + 1];
        ways[0] = 1;  // the empty sequence
        for (int t = 1; t <= target; t++) {  // totals outside: every order is counted
            for (int x : nums) {
                if (x <= t) {
                    ways[t] += ways[t - x];  // sequences ending with x
                }
            }
        }
        return (int) ways[target];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Classifying sequences by their last number gives each sequence exactly once.
  2. Putting the total in the outer loop allows any number at any position, which is why orders count separately.

Medium 396. Rotate Function Google Meta Amazon ArrayMath

Problem: F(k) = Σ i · arrₖ[i] where arrₖ is nums rotated right by k. Return the maximum F(k).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [4,3,2,6]
Output: 26
Explanation: F(0) = (0 * 4) + (1 * 3) + (2 * 2) + (3 * 6) = 0 + 3 + 4 + 18 = 25 F(1) = (0 * 6) + (1 * 4) + (2 * 3) + (3 * 2) = 0 + 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 F(2) = (0 * 2) + (1 * 6) + (2 * 4) + (3 * 3) = 0 + 6 + 8 + 9 = 23 F(3) = (0 * 3) + (1 * 2) + (2 * 6) + (3 * 4) = 0 + 2 + 12 + 12 = 26 So the maximum value of F(0), F(1), F(2), F(3) is F(3) = 26.
Example 2
Input: nums = [100]
Output: 0

Constraints: n == nums.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · -100 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 100

Hint 1

Write out F(1) − F(0). What changes?

Hint 2

Every element gains one coefficient step except the one that wraps around.

From brute force to the pattern: Computing every F(k) directly is O(n²); the recurrence is O(n).

Spot it: Computing each F(k) from scratch is O(n²). Each rotation adds 1 to every coefficient (adding sum) except the last element, which drops from n − 1 to 0 (subtracting n · that element). A recurrence from one state to the next.

Why not another pattern? Direct evaluation of all n rotations is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. F = Σ i · nums[i], total = sum(nums).
  2. For k = 1..n − 1: F += total − n · nums[n − k].
  3. Track the maximum.
class Solution:
    def maxRotateFunction(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        total = sum(nums)
        f = sum(i * x for i, x in enumerate(nums))  # F(0)
        best = f
        for k in range(1, n):
            f += total - n * nums[n - k]  # everyone shifts right; the last element wraps to index 0
            best = max(best, f)
        return best
function maxRotateFunction(nums: number[]): number {
    const n = nums.length;
    const total = nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    let f = nums.reduce((acc, x, i) => acc + i * x, 0);  // F(0)
    let best = f;
    for (let k = 1; k < n; k++) {
        f += total - n * nums[n - k];  // everyone shifts right; the last element wraps to index 0
        best = Math.max(best, f);
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int maxRotateFunction(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int total = 0, f = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            total += nums[i];
            f += i * nums[i];  // F(0)
        }
        int best = f;
        for (int k = 1; k < n; k++) {
            f += total - n * nums[n - k];  // everyone shifts right; the last element wraps to index 0
            best = Math.max(best, f);
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Rotating right moves every element one index up (adding its value once more), so F grows by total.
  2. The element at the end wraps to index 0: it had coefficient n − 1, now 0, a loss of n · value after the total was added.
  3. In rotation k the wrapping element is nums[n − k].

  • Negative numbers.
  • All equal values.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 486. Predict the Winner Google Meta Amazon Cisco Microsoft Array

Problem: Players alternately take a number from either end. Does player 1 win (ties count as a win) with optimal play?

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,5,2]
Output: false
Explanation: Player 1 must open by taking either 1 or 2, and both choices lead to the same result. If Player 1 takes 1, the array becomes [5,2]. Player 2 takes 5, leaving 2 for Player 1. If Player 1 takes 2, the array becomes [1,5]. Player 2 takes 5, leaving 1 for Player 1. Either way, Player 1 finishes with 1 + 2 = 3 and Player 2 finishes with 5. Player 1 can never win, so return false.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,5,233,7]
Output: true
Explanation: Player 1 first takes 1, leaving [5,233,7]. Player 2 must then choose between 5 and 7, and no matter which number Player 2 chooses, Player 1 can take 233 on the next turn. Player 1 finishes with a higher score (234) than Player 2 (12), so return true.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 20 · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁷

Hint 1

Greedy taking the larger end fails. Think in terms of score difference.

Hint 2

Define dp[i][j] = the best difference the current player can get on nums[i..j].

From brute force to the pattern: Exploring the full game tree is O(2ⁿ); the interval DP is O(n²).

Spot it: A two-player game on an interval → interval DP with the score difference: the player to move on nums[i..j] takes one end and then faces the opponent's best difference on what's left.

Why not another pattern? Greedy (take the bigger end) loses on cases like [1, 5, 2] vs [1, 5, 233, 7].

Approach:

  1. diff[i][i] = nums[i].
  2. diff[i][j] = max(nums[i] − diff[i+1][j], nums[j] − diff[i][j−1]).
  3. Player 1 wins if diff[0][n−1] ≥ 0.
class Solution:
    def predictTheWinner(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        n = len(nums)
        diff = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]  # diff[i][j]: mover's score minus opponent's on nums[i..j]
        for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            diff[i][i] = nums[i]
            for j in range(i + 1, n):
                take_left = nums[i] - diff[i + 1][j]  # opponent then plays optimally on the rest
                take_right = nums[j] - diff[i][j - 1]
                diff[i][j] = max(take_left, take_right)
        return diff[0][n - 1] >= 0
function predictTheWinner(nums: number[]): boolean {
    const n = nums.length;
    // diff[i][j]: mover's score minus opponent's on nums[i..j]
    const diff: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0));
    for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        diff[i][i] = nums[i];
        for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            const takeLeft = nums[i] - diff[i + 1][j];  // opponent then plays optimally on the rest
            const takeRight = nums[j] - diff[i][j - 1];
            diff[i][j] = Math.max(takeLeft, takeRight);
        }
    }
    return diff[0][n - 1] >= 0;
}
class Solution {
    public boolean predictTheWinner(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[][] diff = new int[n][n];  // diff[i][j]: mover's score minus opponent's on nums[i..j]
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            diff[i][i] = nums[i];
            for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
                int takeLeft = nums[i] - diff[i + 1][j];  // opponent then plays optimally on the rest
                int takeRight = nums[j] - diff[i][j - 1];
                diff[i][j] = Math.max(takeLeft, takeRight);
            }
        }
        return diff[0][n - 1] >= 0;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Using the difference removes the need to track whose turn it is: the opponent's best difference is subtracted.
  2. Rows go from the bottom up so diff[i + 1][j] is ready before diff[i][j].

  • A tie → true.
  • An even count (player 1 can always at least tie).

Complexity: O(n²) time and space.

Medium 494. Target Sum Google Amazon Microsoft ArrayHash Map

Problem: Put + or − before each number; count the expressions that evaluate to target.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,1,1,1,1], target = 3
Output: 5
Explanation: There are 5 ways to assign symbols to make the sum of nums be target 3. -1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 +1 - 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 +1 + 1 - 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 +1 + 1 + 1 - 1 + 1 = 3 +1 + 1 + 1 + 1 - 1 = 3
Example 2
Input: nums = [1], target = 1
Output: 1

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 20 · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 1000 · 0 ≤ sum(nums[i]) ≤ 1000 · -1000 ≤ target ≤ 1000

Hint 1

What do you need to remember after choosing signs for the first few numbers?

Hint 2

Keep a map from running sum to the number of ways to reach it.

From brute force to the pattern: Enumerating all 2ⁿ sign patterns is exponential; merging equal sums makes it O(n · S).

Spot it: After processing some numbers, only the running sum matters → DP over sums (a hash map from sum to number of ways). Equivalently a 0/1 knapsack: choose the positive set P with sum(P) = (total + target) / 2.

Why not another pattern? Trying all 2ⁿ sign choices is too slow for n = 20 in many languages and doesn't scale.

Approach:

  1. ways = {0: 1}.
  2. For each number x: new map with s + x and s − x for every s, adding counts.
  3. Return ways[target].
from collections import defaultdict

class Solution:
    def findTargetSumWays(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        ways = {0: 1}  # running sum -> number of sign choices giving it
        for x in nums:
            nxt = defaultdict(int)
            for s, count in ways.items():
                nxt[s + x] += count  # put + before x
                nxt[s - x] += count  # put - before x
            ways = nxt
        return ways.get(target, 0)
function findTargetSumWays(nums: number[], target: number): number {
    let ways = new Map<number, number>([[0, 1]]);  // running sum -> number of sign choices giving it
    for (const x of nums) {
        const nxt = new Map<number, number>();
        for (const [s, count] of ways) {
            nxt.set(s + x, (nxt.get(s + x) ?? 0) + count);  // put + before x
            nxt.set(s - x, (nxt.get(s - x) ?? 0) + count);  // put - before x
        }
        ways = nxt;
    }
    return ways.get(target) ?? 0;
}
class Solution {
    public int findTargetSumWays(int[] nums, int target) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> ways = new HashMap<>();  // running sum -> number of sign choices giving it
        ways.put(0, 1);
        for (int x : nums) {
            Map<Integer, Integer> nxt = new HashMap<>();
            for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : ways.entrySet()) {
                int s = e.getKey(), count = e.getValue();
                nxt.merge(s + x, count, Integer::sum);  // put + before x
                nxt.merge(s - x, count, Integer::sum);  // put - before x
            }
            ways = nxt;
        }
        return ways.getOrDefault(target, 0);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Different sign choices that reach the same sum are merged, so the state space is bounded by the range of sums.
  2. Zeros double the count (both signs give the same sum), which the map handles naturally.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Zeros (both signs count).
  • Unreachable target → 0.
  • Negative target.

Complexity: O(n · S) time and space, where S is the range of possible sums (≤ 2·sum + 1).

Medium 516. Longest Palindromic Subsequence Google Meta Amazon Microsoft String

Problem: Return the length of the longest palindromic subsequence of s.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "bbbab"
Output: 4
Explanation: One possible longest palindromic subsequence is "bbbb".
Example 2
Input: s = "cbbd"
Output: 2
Explanation: One possible longest palindromic subsequence is "bb".

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 1000 · s consists only of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

Think about the first and last characters of the range.

Hint 2

If they match they can both be in the palindrome; if not, drop one.

From brute force to the pattern: All subsequences: O(2ⁿ). Interval DP: O(n²).

Spot it: A palindrome is decided by its outer pair, then its inside → interval DP on s[i..j]. Equal ends both join; different ends mean one of them isn't used.

Why not another pattern? Checking all 2ⁿ subsequences is impossible; it also equals LCS(s, reversed s) but the interval form is direct.

Approach:

  1. L[i][i] = 1.
  2. s[i] == s[j]: L[i][j] = L[i+1][j−1] + 2; else max(L[i+1][j], L[i][j−1]).
class Solution:
    def longestPalindromeSubseq(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        L = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]  # L[i][j]: longest palindromic subsequence in s[i..j]
        for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            L[i][i] = 1
            for j in range(i + 1, n):
                if s[i] == s[j]:
                    L[i][j] = L[i + 1][j - 1] + 2  # both ends wrap the inside
                else:
                    L[i][j] = max(L[i + 1][j], L[i][j - 1])  # one end can't be used
        return L[0][n - 1]
function longestPalindromeSubseq(s: string): number {
    const n = s.length;
    // L[i][j]: longest palindromic subsequence in s[i..j]
    const L: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0));
    for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        L[i][i] = 1;
        for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (s[i] === s[j]) {
                L[i][j] = L[i + 1][j - 1] + 2;  // both ends wrap the inside
            } else {
                L[i][j] = Math.max(L[i + 1][j], L[i][j - 1]);  // one end can't be used
            }
        }
    }
    return L[0][n - 1];
}
class Solution {
    public int longestPalindromeSubseq(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        int[][] L = new int[n][n];  // L[i][j]: longest palindromic subsequence in s[i..j]
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            L[i][i] = 1;
            for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
                if (s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j)) {
                    L[i][j] = L[i + 1][j - 1] + 2;  // both ends wrap the inside
                } else {
                    L[i][j] = Math.max(L[i + 1][j], L[i][j - 1]);  // one end can't be used
                }
            }
        }
        return L[0][n - 1];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Rows from bottom to top make L[i + 1][…] ready first.
  2. When j = i + 1 and the characters match, L[i + 1][j − 1] is the empty range (0).

  • All distinct → 1.
  • Length 1.

Complexity: O(n²) time and space.

Hint 1

Hint 2

From brute force to the pattern: Trying all subsets to delete is exponential; LCS is O(mn).

Spot it: What remains in both strings is a common subsequence; to delete least, keep the longest one → LCS DP.

Why not another pattern? Edit distance with replacements gives a different (smaller) number; only deletions are allowed here.

Approach:

  1. LCS table: L[i][j] = L[i−1][j−1] + 1 if chars match else max(L[i−1][j], L[i][j−1]).
  2. Answer: m + n − 2 · L[m][n].
class Solution:
    def minDistance(self, word1: str, word2: str) -> int:
        m, n = len(word1), len(word2)
        L = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]  # L[i][j]: LCS of word1[:i], word2[:j]
        for i in range(1, m + 1):
            for j in range(1, n + 1):
                if word1[i - 1] == word2[j - 1]:
                    L[i][j] = L[i - 1][j - 1] + 1  # keep this common letter
                else:
                    L[i][j] = max(L[i - 1][j], L[i][j - 1])
        return m + n - 2 * L[m][n]  # delete everything outside the LCS
function minDistance(word1: string, word2: string): number {
    const m = word1.length, n = word2.length;
    // L[i][j]: LCS of the first i letters of word1 and the first j of word2
    const L: number[][] = Array.from({ length: m + 1 }, () => new Array(n + 1).fill(0));
    for (let i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (let j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            if (word1[i - 1] === word2[j - 1]) {
                L[i][j] = L[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;  // keep this common letter
            } else {
                L[i][j] = Math.max(L[i - 1][j], L[i][j - 1]);
            }
        }
    }
    return m + n - 2 * L[m][n];  // delete everything outside the LCS
}
class Solution {
    public int minDistance(String word1, String word2) {
        int m = word1.length(), n = word2.length();
        int[][] L = new int[m + 1][n + 1];  // L[i][j]: LCS of the first i letters of word1 and the first j of word2
        for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
                if (word1.charAt(i - 1) == word2.charAt(j - 1)) {
                    L[i][j] = L[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;  // keep this common letter
                } else {
                    L[i][j] = Math.max(L[i - 1][j], L[i][j - 1]);
                }
            }
        }
        return m + n - 2 * L[m][n];  // delete everything outside the LCS
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The final common string must be a subsequence of both words.
  2. Keeping the LCS minimises the letters deleted from each side.

Medium 638. Shopping Offers Google ArrayHash Map

Problem: Buy exactly the needed quantities of up to 6 items using single prices and bundle offers. Return the minimum cost.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: price = [2,5], special = [[3,0,5],[1,2,10]], needs = [3,2]
Output: 14
Explanation: There are two kinds of items, A and B. Their prices are $2 and $5 respectively. In special offer 1, you can pay $5 for 3A and 0B In special offer 2, you can pay $10 for 1A and 2B. You need to buy 3A and 2B, so you may pay $10 for 1A and 2B (special offer #2), and $4 for 2A.
Example 2
Input: price = [2,3,4], special = [[1,1,0,4],[2,2,1,9]], needs = [1,2,1]
Output: 11
Explanation: The price of A is $2, and $3 for B, $4 for C. You may pay $4 for 1A and 1B, and $9 for 2A ,2B and 1C. You need to buy 1A ,2B and 1C, so you may pay $4 for 1A and 1B (special offer #1), and $3 for 1B, $4 for 1C. You cannot add more items, though only $9 for 2A ,2B and 1C.

Constraints: n == price.length == needs.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 6 · 0 ≤ price[i], needs[i] ≤ 10 · 1 ≤ special.length ≤ 100 · special[i].length == n + 1 · 0 ≤ special[i][j] ≤ 50 · The input is generated that at least one of special[i][j] is non-zero for 0 ≤ j ≤ n - 1.

Hint 1

The needs are small. What should the state of a recursion be?

Hint 2

From a state, either buy the rest at single prices or apply one offer and recurse; memoise.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every sequence of offers without memo repeats states; the memo bounds the work by the number of need vectors.

Spot it: The state is the vector of remaining needs (small: ≤ 6 items, ≤ 10 each) → memoised DP over tuples. From a state, either pay full price for everything or apply an offer that fits and recurse.

Why not another pattern? Greedy (best discount first) fails because offers interact.

Approach:

  1. cost(needs): start with buying everything at single prices.
  2. For each offer that doesn't exceed any need: offer price + cost(needs − offer).
  3. Memoise on the needs tuple.
from functools import lru_cache

class Solution:
    def shoppingOffers(self, price: List[int], special: List[List[int]], needs: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(price)

        @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
        def cost(needs):
            best = sum(p * q for p, q in zip(price, needs))  # no offers: buy singly
            for offer in special:
                rest = tuple(needs[i] - offer[i] for i in range(n))
                if min(rest) >= 0:  # the offer doesn't give more than needed
                    best = min(best, offer[n] + cost(rest))
            return best

        return cost(tuple(needs))
function shoppingOffers(price: number[], special: number[][], needs: number[]): number {
    const n = price.length;
    const memo = new Map<string, number>();

    const cost = (needs: number[]): number => {
        const key = needs.join(",");
        if (memo.has(key)) {
            return memo.get(key)!;
        }
        let best = price.reduce((acc, p, i) => acc + p * needs[i], 0);  // no offers: buy singly
        for (const offer of special) {
            const rest = needs.map((q, i) => q - offer[i]);
            if (Math.min(...rest) >= 0) {  // the offer doesn't give more than needed
                best = Math.min(best, offer[n] + cost(rest));
            }
        }
        memo.set(key, best);
        return best;
    };

    return cost(needs);
}
class Solution {
    private List<Integer> price;
    private List<List<Integer>> special;
    private Map<List<Integer>, Integer> memo;

    public int shoppingOffers(List<Integer> price, List<List<Integer>> special, List<Integer> needs) {
        this.price = price;
        this.special = special;
        memo = new HashMap<>();
        return cost(needs);
    }

    private int cost(List<Integer> needs) {
        if (memo.containsKey(needs)) {
            return memo.get(needs);
        }
        int n = price.size();
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            best += price.get(i) * needs.get(i);  // no offers: buy singly
        }
        for (List<Integer> offer : special) {
            List<Integer> rest = new ArrayList<>();
            boolean fits = true;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                rest.add(needs.get(i) - offer.get(i));
                if (rest.get(i) < 0) {
                    fits = false;
                }
            }
            if (fits) {  // the offer doesn't give more than needed
                best = Math.min(best, offer.get(n) + cost(rest));
            }
        }
        memo.put(needs, best);
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each state is a tuple, so it can be a cache key.
  2. Offers that would overshoot any item are skipped (buying extra isn't allowed).
  3. The number of states is at most 11⁶, and much less in practice.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • An offer more expensive than buying singly.
  • No offer fits.
  • Needs all zero → 0.

Complexity: O(S · offers · n) time, where S is the number of reachable needs vectors.

Medium 647. Palindromic Substrings Google Meta Amazon Cisco Microsoft String

Problem: Count the substrings of s that are palindromes.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "abc"
Output: 3
Explanation: Three palindromic strings: "a", "b", "c".
Example 2
Input: s = "aaa"
Output: 6
Explanation: Six palindromic strings: "a", "a", "a", "aa", "aa", "aaa".

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 1000 · s consists of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

A palindrome is determined by its centre and radius.

Hint 2

Expand around each of the 2n − 1 centres.

From brute force to the pattern: Testing every substring is O(n³); centre expansion is O(n²).

Spot it: A palindrome grows from its centre: s[l..r] is one if s[l+1..r−1] is and s[l] == s[r]. Expanding around every centre applies that DP relation without a table.

Why not another pattern? Checking each of the O(n²) substrings separately is O(n³).

Approach:

  1. For each centre (a character, or a gap between two): l, r start there.
  2. While s[l] == s[r]: count one, expand outwards.
class Solution:
    def countSubstrings(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        count = 0
        for center in range(2 * n - 1):  # n letters and n - 1 gaps
            l = center // 2
            r = l + center % 2
            while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
                count += 1  # s[l..r] is a palindrome
                l -= 1
                r += 1
        return count
function countSubstrings(s: string): number {
    const n = s.length;
    let count = 0;
    for (let center = 0; center < 2 * n - 1; center++) {  // n letters and n - 1 gaps
        let l = Math.floor(center / 2);
        let r = l + (center % 2);
        while (l >= 0 && r < n && s[l] === s[r]) {
            count += 1;  // s[l..r] is a palindrome
            l -= 1;
            r += 1;
        }
    }
    return count;
}
class Solution {
    public int countSubstrings(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        int count = 0;
        for (int center = 0; center < 2 * n - 1; center++) {  // n letters and n - 1 gaps
            int l = center / 2;
            int r = l + center % 2;
            while (l >= 0 && r < n && s.charAt(l) == s.charAt(r)) {
                count += 1;  // s[l..r] is a palindrome
                l -= 1;
                r += 1;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Even center values are letters (odd-length palindromes); odd values are gaps (even length).
  2. Every expansion step is a new palindrome with the same centre.

  • All distinct → n.
  • Single character.

Complexity: O(n²) time, O(1) space.

Medium 673. Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence Google Amazon Array

Problem: Return how many longest strictly increasing subsequences there are.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,3,5,4,7]
Output: 2
Explanation: The two longest increasing subsequences are [1, 3, 4, 7] and [1, 3, 5, 7].
Example 2
Input: nums = [2,2,2,2,2]
Output: 5
Explanation: The length of the longest increasing subsequence is 1, and there are 5 increasing subsequences of length 1, so output 5.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 2000 · -10⁶ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁶ · The answer is guaranteed to fit inside a 32-bit integer.

Hint 1

Start from the O(n²) LIS DP.

Hint 2

Alongside the length, keep how many subsequences reach that length.

From brute force to the pattern: Listing every increasing subsequence is exponential; the counting DP is O(n²).

Spot it: The O(n²) LIS DP extended with counts: length[i] and count[i] for subsequences ending at i. A longer extension resets the count; an equally long one adds to it.

Why not another pattern? The patience-sorting O(n log n) LIS gives the length but not the count without extra structure.

Approach:

  1. length[i] = count[i] = 1.
  2. For j < i with nums[j] < nums[i]: if length[j] + 1 > length[i], take it and copy count[j]; if equal, add count[j].
  3. Sum count[i] over indices with the maximum length.
class Solution:
    def findNumberOfLIS(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(nums)
        length = [1] * n  # longest increasing subsequence ending at i
        count = [1] * n  # how many of that length end at i
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i):
                if nums[j] < nums[i]:
                    if length[j] + 1 > length[i]:
                        length[i] = length[j] + 1  # a longer one: restart the count
                        count[i] = count[j]
                    elif length[j] + 1 == length[i]:
                        count[i] += count[j]  # another way to the same length
        top = max(length)
        return sum(c for l, c in zip(length, count) if l == top)
function findNumberOfLIS(nums: number[]): number {
    const n = nums.length;
    const length: number[] = new Array(n).fill(1);  // longest increasing subsequence ending at i
    const count: number[] = new Array(n).fill(1);   // how many of that length end at i
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (let j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (nums[j] < nums[i]) {
                if (length[j] + 1 > length[i]) {
                    length[i] = length[j] + 1;  // a longer one: restart the count
                    count[i] = count[j];
                } else if (length[j] + 1 === length[i]) {
                    count[i] += count[j];  // another way to the same length
                }
            }
        }
    }
    const top = Math.max(...length);
    return count.reduce((acc, c, i) => acc + (length[i] === top ? c : 0), 0);
}
class Solution {
    public int findNumberOfLIS(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] length = new int[n];  // longest increasing subsequence ending at i
        int[] count = new int[n];   // how many of that length end at i
        Arrays.fill(length, 1);
        Arrays.fill(count, 1);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
                if (nums[j] < nums[i]) {
                    if (length[j] + 1 > length[i]) {
                        length[i] = length[j] + 1;  // a longer one: restart the count
                        count[i] = count[j];
                    } else if (length[j] + 1 == length[i]) {
                        count[i] += count[j];  // another way to the same length
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        int top = Arrays.stream(length).max().getAsInt();
        int total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (length[i] == top) {
                total += count[i];
            }
        }
        return total;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. count[i] counts distinct index sequences, matching the problem's definition.
  2. The final answer adds the counts over every possible ending index.

Edge cases to test:

  • All equal → n (each element alone).
  • Strictly increasing → 1.
  • Decreasing → n.

Complexity: O(n²) time, O(n) space.

Medium 714. Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee Google Apple Array

Problem: Unlimited transactions, each costing fee. Return the maximum profit.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: prices = [1,3,2,8,4,9], fee = 2
Output: 8
Explanation: The maximum profit can be achieved by: - Buying at prices[0] = 1 - Selling at prices[3] = 8 - Buying at prices[4] = 4 - Selling at prices[5] = 9 The total profit is ((8 - 1) - 2) + ((9 - 4) - 2) = 8.
Example 2
Input: prices = [1,3,7,5,10,3], fee = 3
Output: 6

Constraints: 1 ≤ prices.length ≤ 5 * 10⁴ · 1 ≤ prices[i] < 5 * 10⁴ · 0 ≤ fee < 5 * 10⁴

Hint 1

What two situations can you be in at the end of each day?

Hint 2

Track the best balance holding and not holding a share.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying all buy/sell day choices is exponential; two states per day is O(n).

Spot it: Each day you either hold a share or don't → two-state DP. Selling moves hold → cash and pays the fee.

Why not another pattern? Adding every price rise (unlimited transactions without fee) pays the fee on each small rise.

Approach:

  1. cash = 0, hold = −prices[0].
  2. Each day: cash = max(cash, hold + p − fee), hold = max(hold, cash − p).
class Solution:
    def maxProfit(self, prices: List[int], fee: int) -> int:
        cash = 0  # best balance with no share
        hold = -prices[0]  # best balance holding a share
        for p in prices[1:]:
            cash = max(cash, hold + p - fee)  # sell today (pay the fee)
            hold = max(hold, cash - p)  # buy today
        return cash
function maxProfit(prices: number[], fee: number): number {
    let cash = 0;            // best balance with no share
    let hold = -prices[0];   // best balance holding a share
    for (const p of prices.slice(1)) {
        cash = Math.max(cash, hold + p - fee);  // sell today (pay the fee)
        hold = Math.max(hold, cash - p);        // buy today
    }
    return cash;
}
class Solution {
    public int maxProfit(int[] prices, int fee) {
        int cash = 0;            // best balance with no share
        int hold = -prices[0];   // best balance holding a share
        for (int i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) {
            int p = prices[i];
            cash = Math.max(cash, hold + p - fee);  // sell today (pay the fee)
            hold = Math.max(hold, cash - p);        // buy today
        }
        return cash;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Using the updated cash for hold on the same day only allows sell-then-buy on one day, which never helps, so it's safe.
  2. The fee makes merging nearby rises into one transaction better, which the DP finds automatically.

  • Fee larger than any rise → 0.
  • Falling prices → 0.
  • One day.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 740. Delete and Earn Google Amazon Microsoft ArrayHash Map

Problem: Taking a number x earns x but deletes every x − 1 and x + 1. Return the maximum points.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [3,4,2]
Output: 6
Explanation: You can perform the following operations: - Delete 4 to earn 4 points. Consequently, 3 is also deleted. nums = [2]. - Delete 2 to earn 2 points. nums = []. You earn a total of 6 points.
Example 2
Input: nums = [2,2,3,3,3,4]
Output: 9
Explanation: You can perform the following operations: - Delete a 3 to earn 3 points. All 2's and 4's are also deleted. nums = [3,3]. - Delete a 3 again to earn 3 points. nums = [3]. - Delete a 3 once more to earn 3 points. nums = []. You earn a total of 9 points.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 2 * 10⁴ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

If you take one x, should you take all of them?

Hint 2

Group by value. Which known problem has "can't pick neighbours"?

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every subset of values is exponential; the House Robber DP is linear in the value range.

Spot it: If you take one x, take them all. Sum points per value: points[x] = x · count(x). Taking x forbids x − 1 and x + 1, which is exactly House Robber on the value line.

Why not another pattern? Greedy (take the biggest total first) fails when two neighbours together beat the middle value.

Approach:

  1. points[v] = v · count(v) for v up to max(nums).
  2. House Robber: take, skip running values; take = skip + points[v], skip = max(previous take, previous skip).
from collections import Counter

class Solution:
    def deleteAndEarn(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        count = Counter(nums)
        take = skip = 0  # best total when value v-1 is taken / not taken
        for v in range(1, max(nums) + 1):
            gain = v * count[v]  # take every copy of v
            take, skip = skip + gain, max(take, skip)  # taking v needs v-1 skipped
        return max(take, skip)
function deleteAndEarn(nums: number[]): number {
    const count = new Map<number, number>();
    for (const x of nums) {
        count.set(x, (count.get(x) ?? 0) + 1);
    }
    let take = 0, skip = 0;  // best total when value v-1 is taken / not taken
    for (let v = 1; v <= Math.max(...nums); v++) {
        const gain = v * (count.get(v) ?? 0);  // take every copy of v
        [take, skip] = [skip + gain, Math.max(take, skip)];  // taking v needs v-1 skipped
    }
    return Math.max(take, skip);
}
class Solution {
    public int deleteAndEarn(int[] nums) {
        int top = Arrays.stream(nums).max().getAsInt();
        int[] count = new int[top + 1];
        for (int x : nums) {
            count[x] += 1;
        }
        int take = 0, skip = 0;  // best total when value v-1 is taken / not taken
        for (int v = 1; v <= top; v++) {
            int gain = v * count[v];  // take every copy of v
            int newTake = skip + gain;  // taking v needs v-1 skipped
            skip = Math.max(take, skip);
            take = newTake;
        }
        return Math.max(take, skip);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Taking one copy of x already deletes all x ± 1, so the other copies of x are free to take too.
  2. Values form a line where neighbours conflict: House Robber.

Edge cases to test:

  • Values with gaps (no conflict).
  • All the same value.
  • One number.

Complexity: O(n + max) time, O(n) space for the counter.

Medium 788. Rotated Digits Google Amazon Math

Problem: A number is good if rotating each digit 180° gives a valid, different number. Count good numbers in 1..n.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 10
Output: 4
Explanation: There are four good numbers in the range [1, 10] : 2, 5, 6, 9. Note that 1 and 10 are not good numbers, since they remain unchanged after rotating.
Example 2
Input: n = 1
Output: 0

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

Classify digits into: rotate to themselves, rotate to another digit, invalid.

Hint 2

A number's class depends on its prefix's class and its last digit.

From brute force to the pattern: Examining every digit of every number is O(n log n); prefix reuse makes it O(n) (digit DP gives O(log n)).

Spot it: Digits 0, 1, 8 rotate to themselves; 2, 5, 6, 9 change; 3, 4, 7 break the number. A number's status follows from i // 10's status and its last digit → DP over numbers (a simple digit DP).

Why not another pattern? Checking each number's digits separately is O(n log n); reusing the prefix status is O(n).

Approach:

  1. state[i]: 0 = invalid, 1 = valid and unchanged, 2 = valid and changed. state[0] = 1.
  2. state[i] = invalid if the last digit is 3/4/7 or the prefix is invalid; changed if either is changed; else unchanged.
  3. Count i ≤ n with state[i] == 2.
class Solution:
    def rotatedDigits(self, n: int) -> int:
        kind = {0: 1, 1: 1, 8: 1, 2: 2, 5: 2, 6: 2, 9: 2, 3: 0, 4: 0, 7: 0}  # 0 bad, 1 same, 2 changes
        state = [0] * (n + 1)
        state[0] = 1
        good = 0
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            prefix, last = state[i // 10], kind[i % 10]
            if prefix == 0 or last == 0:
                state[i] = 0  # contains 3, 4 or 7
            else:
                state[i] = max(prefix, last)  # changed if any digit changes
            if state[i] == 2:
                good += 1
        return good
function rotatedDigits(n: number): number {
    const kind = [1, 1, 2, 0, 0, 2, 2, 0, 1, 2];  // by digit: 0 bad, 1 same, 2 changes
    const state: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(0);
    state[0] = 1;
    let good = 0;
    for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        const prefix = state[Math.floor(i / 10)], last = kind[i % 10];
        if (prefix === 0 || last === 0) {
            state[i] = 0;  // contains 3, 4 or 7
        } else {
            state[i] = Math.max(prefix, last);  // changed if any digit changes
        }
        if (state[i] === 2) {
            good += 1;
        }
    }
    return good;
}
class Solution {
    public int rotatedDigits(int n) {
        int[] kind = {1, 1, 2, 0, 0, 2, 2, 0, 1, 2};  // by digit: 0 bad, 1 same, 2 changes
        int[] state = new int[n + 1];
        state[0] = 1;
        int good = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            int prefix = state[i / 10], last = kind[i % 10];
            if (prefix == 0 || last == 0) {
                state[i] = 0;  // contains 3, 4 or 7
            } else {
                state[i] = Math.max(prefix, last);  // changed if any digit changes
            }
            if (state[i] == 2) {
                good += 1;
            }
        }
        return good;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. i // 10 is i without its last digit, already computed.
  2. Using 0 < 1 < 2 for bad < same < changed makes max the right combination once both parts are valid.

  • Numbers made only of 0/1/8 (valid but unchanged).
  • Any 3/4/7 digit.

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Medium 790. Domino and Tromino Tiling Google Amazon Math

Problem: Count tilings of a 2 × n board with dominoes and L-trominoes (mod 10⁹ + 7).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 3
Output: 5
Explanation: The five different ways are shown above.
Example 2
Input: n = 1
Output: 1

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 1000

Hint 1

Besides a flat edge, what other edge shapes can a partial tiling have?

Hint 2

Track full coverage and "one cell sticking out"; write transitions between them.

From brute force to the pattern: Enumerating tilings is exponential; two states per column make it linear.

Spot it: Tile column by column. Besides a flat edge, a tromino can leave one cell sticking out, so track two states: full[i] (first i columns covered) and half[i] (first i columns plus one cell of column i + 1; top and bottom are mirror images, so count one and double it) → DP with profile states.

Why not another pattern? Counting with dominoes only (Fibonacci) misses tromino pairs that span several columns.

Approach:

  1. full[0] = full[1] = 1, half[0] = 0, half[1] = 1.
  2. full[i] = full[i−1] (vertical domino) + full[i−2] (two horizontal dominoes) + 2 · half[i−2] (a tromino fills the gap and column i).
  3. half[i] = full[i−1] (a tromino covers column i and sticks out) + half[i−1] (a horizontal domino fills the gap and sticks out).
class Solution:
    def numTilings(self, n: int) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        full = [0] * (n + 1)  # columns 1..i fully covered
        half = [0] * (n + 1)  # columns 1..i covered plus one cell of column i+1 (one orientation)
        full[0] = 1
        full[1] = 1
        half[1] = 1  # a tromino covering column 1 and one cell of column 2
        for i in range(2, n + 1):
            full[i] = (full[i - 1] + full[i - 2] + 2 * half[i - 2]) % MOD  # domino, two dominoes, or a closing tromino
            half[i] = (full[i - 1] + half[i - 1]) % MOD  # open with a tromino, or extend with a domino
        return full[n]
function numTilings(n: number): number {
    const MOD = 1_000_000_007;
    const full: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(0);  // columns 1..i fully covered
    const half: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(0);  // columns 1..i covered plus one cell of column i+1 (one orientation)
    full[0] = 1;
    full[1] = 1;
    half[1] = 1;  // a tromino covering column 1 and one cell of column 2
    for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        full[i] = (full[i - 1] + full[i - 2] + 2 * half[i - 2]) % MOD;  // domino, two dominoes, or a closing tromino
        half[i] = (full[i - 1] + half[i - 1]) % MOD;  // open with a tromino, or extend with a domino
    }
    return full[n];
}
class Solution {
    public int numTilings(int n) {
        final long MOD = 1_000_000_007;
        long[] full = new long[n + 1];  // columns 1..i fully covered
        long[] half = new long[n + 1];  // columns 1..i covered plus one cell of column i+1 (one orientation)
        full[0] = 1;
        full[1] = 1;
        half[1] = 1;  // a tromino covering column 1 and one cell of column 2
        for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
            full[i] = (full[i - 1] + full[i - 2] + 2 * half[i - 2]) % MOD;  // domino, two dominoes, or a closing tromino
            half[i] = (full[i - 1] + half[i - 1]) % MOD;  // open with a tromino, or extend with a domino
        }
        return (int) full[n];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The jagged edge has two mirror images (top or bottom cell sticking out); half counts one and the factor 2 covers both.
  2. From a jagged state ending at column i − 2 with one cell in column i − 1, a tromino covers the other cell of i − 1 and all of column i.
  3. A jagged state is created by a tromino on a flat edge, or carried forward by a horizontal domino in the empty row.

  • n = 2 → 2.
  • n = 3 → 5 (includes tromino pairs).

Complexity: O(n) time (O(1) space if only the last values are kept).

Medium 799. Champagne Tower Google Array

Problem: Pour poured cups on the top glass of a pyramid; overflow splits equally to the two glasses below. How full is glass (query_row, query_glass)?

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: poured = 1, query_row = 1, query_glass = 1
Output: 0.00000
Explanation: We poured 1 cup of champange to the top glass of the tower (which is indexed as (0, 0)). There will be no excess liquid so all the glasses under the top glass will remain empty.
Example 2
Input: poured = 2, query_row = 1, query_glass = 1
Output: 0.50000
Explanation: We poured 2 cups of champange to the top glass of the tower (which is indexed as (0, 0)). There is one cup of excess liquid. The glass indexed as (1, 0) and the glass indexed as (1, 1) will share the excess liquid equally, and each will get half cup of champange.

Constraints: 0 ≤ poured ≤ 10⁹ · 0 ≤ query_glass ≤ query_row < 100

Hint 1

Track how much liquid flows into each glass, not just how full it is.

Hint 2

Each glass passes (flow − 1) / 2 to each of its two children.

From brute force to the pattern: Pouring one cup at a time and simulating is slower and unnecessary. Row DP is O(rows²).

Spot it: Flow only goes down, so each row depends on the row above → row-by-row DP of how much liquid passes through each glass.

Why not another pattern? Simulating cup by cup over time is unnecessary; only the total flow through each glass matters.

Approach:

  1. row = [poured].
  2. For each next row: every glass with x > 1 sends (x − 1) / 2 to each child.
  3. Return min(1, row[query_glass]).
class Solution:
    def champagneTower(self, poured: int, query_row: int, query_glass: int) -> float:
        row = [float(poured)]  # total liquid that reaches each glass of the current row
        for r in range(query_row):
            nxt = [0.0] * (r + 2)
            for i, x in enumerate(row):
                extra = max(0.0, x - 1) / 2  # the glass keeps 1 cup; the rest splits
                nxt[i] += extra
                nxt[i + 1] += extra
            row = nxt
        return min(1.0, row[query_glass])
function champagneTower(poured: number, query_row: number, query_glass: number): number {
    let row: number[] = [poured];  // total liquid that reaches each glass of the current row
    for (let r = 0; r < query_row; r++) {
        const nxt: number[] = new Array(r + 2).fill(0);
        row.forEach((x, i) => {
            const extra = Math.max(0, x - 1) / 2;  // the glass keeps 1 cup; the rest splits
            nxt[i] += extra;
            nxt[i + 1] += extra;
        });
        row = nxt;
    }
    return Math.min(1, row[query_glass]);
}
class Solution {
    public double champagneTower(int poured, int query_row, int query_glass) {
        double[] row = {poured};  // total liquid that reaches each glass of the current row
        for (int r = 0; r < query_row; r++) {
            double[] nxt = new double[r + 2];
            for (int i = 0; i < row.length; i++) {
                double extra = Math.max(0.0, row[i] - 1) / 2;  // the glass keeps 1 cup; the rest splits
                nxt[i] += extra;
                nxt[i + 1] += extra;
            }
            row = nxt;
        }
        return Math.min(1.0, row[query_glass]);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The value stored is the total that flows into a glass, which may exceed 1.
  2. Only the excess over 1 is shared, half to each child.
  3. The answer is capped at 1, a full glass.

  • A glass at the edge of a row (one parent).
  • Huge poured (cap at 1).

Complexity: O(query_row²) time, O(query_row) space.

Medium 877. Stone Game Google Meta Microsoft Array

Problem: Even number of piles, odd total; players take a pile from either end. Does Alice (first) win with optimal play?

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: piles = [5,3,4,5]
Output: true
Explanation: Alice starts first, and can only take the first 5 or the last 5. Say she takes the first 5, so that the row becomes [3, 4, 5]. If Bob takes 3, then the board is [4, 5], and Alice takes 5 to win with 10 points. If Bob takes the last 5, then the board is [3, 4], and Alice takes 4 to win with 9 points. This demonstrated that taking the first 5 was a winning move for Alice, so we return true.
Example 2
Input: piles = [3,7,2,3]
Output: true

Constraints: 2 ≤ piles.length ≤ 500 · piles.length is even. · 1 ≤ piles[i] ≤ 500 · sum(piles[i]) is odd.

Hint 1

Think of the score difference between the player to move and the other.

Hint 2

Bonus: with an even number of piles, can Alice force taking all even-indexed piles?

From brute force to the pattern: The full game tree is O(2ⁿ); interval DP is O(n²).

Spot it: Same game as Predict the Winner → interval DP on the score difference. (There's also a proof: Alice can choose to take all even-indexed or all odd-indexed piles, and one of those sums is larger, so she always wins.)

Why not another pattern? Greedy (take the larger end) isn't optimal; return True is correct but the DP shows why.

Approach:

  1. diff[i][j] = best (mover − other) on piles i..j.
  2. diff[i][j] = max(piles[i] − diff[i+1][j], piles[j] − diff[i][j−1]).
  3. Return diff[0][n−1] > 0.
class Solution:
    def stoneGame(self, piles: List[int]) -> bool:
        n = len(piles)
        diff = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]  # mover's lead on piles[i..j]
        for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            diff[i][i] = piles[i]
            for j in range(i + 1, n):
                diff[i][j] = max(piles[i] - diff[i + 1][j], piles[j] - diff[i][j - 1])  # take an end
        return diff[0][n - 1] > 0
function stoneGame(piles: number[]): boolean {
    const n = piles.length;
    const diff: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0));  // mover's lead on piles[i..j]
    for (let i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        diff[i][i] = piles[i];
        for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            diff[i][j] = Math.max(piles[i] - diff[i + 1][j], piles[j] - diff[i][j - 1]);  // take an end
        }
    }
    return diff[0][n - 1] > 0;
}
class Solution {
    public boolean stoneGame(int[] piles) {
        int n = piles.length;
        int[][] diff = new int[n][n];  // mover's lead on piles[i..j]
        for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            diff[i][i] = piles[i];
            for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
                diff[i][j] = Math.max(piles[i] - diff[i + 1][j], piles[j] - diff[i][j - 1]);  // take an end
            }
        }
        return diff[0][n - 1] > 0;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each choice gives the opponent the remaining interval, where they get their own best lead.
  2. The total is odd, so there are no ties; a positive lead means Alice wins.

  • Large middle pile.
  • Alternating big and small piles.

Medium 918. Maximum Sum Circular Subarray Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Return the maximum sum of a non-empty subarray of a circular array.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,-2,3,-2]
Output: 3
Explanation: Subarray [3] has maximum sum 3.
Example 2
Input: nums = [5,-3,5]
Output: 10
Explanation: Subarray [5,5] has maximum sum 5 + 5 = 10.

Constraints: n == nums.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 3 * 10⁴ · -3 * 10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 3 * 10⁴

Hint 1

A subarray that wraps around is the complement of a subarray in the middle.

Hint 2

Run Kadane for both the maximum and the minimum subarray.

From brute force to the pattern: Kadane from every starting point is O(n²); the complement trick is O(n).

Spot it: A wrapping subarray is the whole array minus a middle subarray, so its best sum is total − (minimum subarray). Run Kadane's DP for both the max and the min.

Why not another pattern? Trying every start point with Kadane is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. Kadane for the maximum subarray and for the minimum subarray, in one pass.
  2. If the max is negative (all numbers negative), return it.
  3. Otherwise return max(max_sub, total − min_sub).
class Solution:
    def maxSubarraySumCircular(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        cur_max = cur_min = 0
        best_max = float("-inf")
        best_min = float("inf")
        for x in nums:
            cur_max = max(cur_max + x, x)  # best subarray ending here
            cur_min = min(cur_min + x, x)  # worst subarray ending here
            best_max = max(best_max, cur_max)
            best_min = min(best_min, cur_min)
        if best_max < 0:
            return best_max  # all negative: removing the min would leave nothing
        return max(best_max, sum(nums) - best_min)  # normal, or wrapping around
function maxSubarraySumCircular(nums: number[]): number {
    let curMax = 0, curMin = 0;
    let bestMax = -Infinity;
    let bestMin = Infinity;
    for (const x of nums) {
        curMax = Math.max(curMax + x, x);  // best subarray ending here
        curMin = Math.min(curMin + x, x);  // worst subarray ending here
        bestMax = Math.max(bestMax, curMax);
        bestMin = Math.min(bestMin, curMin);
    }
    if (bestMax < 0) {
        return bestMax;  // all negative: removing the min would leave nothing
    }
    const total = nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    return Math.max(bestMax, total - bestMin);  // normal, or wrapping around
}
class Solution {
    public int maxSubarraySumCircular(int[] nums) {
        int curMax = 0, curMin = 0;
        int bestMax = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        int bestMin = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int total = 0;
        for (int x : nums) {
            curMax = Math.max(curMax + x, x);  // best subarray ending here
            curMin = Math.min(curMin + x, x);  // worst subarray ending here
            bestMax = Math.max(bestMax, curMax);
            bestMin = Math.min(bestMin, curMin);
            total += x;
        }
        if (bestMax < 0) {
            return bestMax;  // all negative: removing the min would leave nothing
        }
        return Math.max(bestMax, total - bestMin);  // normal, or wrapping around
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A wrapping subarray leaves out one contiguous middle part; leaving out the smallest one gives the biggest wrap.
  2. If every number is negative, total − min would be the empty subarray (0), which isn't allowed.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

  • All positive (the whole array).
  • One element.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 931. Minimum Falling Path Sum Google Amazon Matrix

Problem: A falling path takes one cell per row, moving to the same or an adjacent column. Return the minimum path sum.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: matrix = [[2,1,3],[6,5,4],[7,8,9]]
Output: 13
Explanation: There are two falling paths with a minimum sum as shown.
Example 2
Input: matrix = [[-19,57],[-40,-5]]
Output: -59
Explanation: The falling path with a minimum sum is shown.

Constraints: n == matrix.length == matrix[i].length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 · -100 ≤ matrix[i][j] ≤ 100

Hint 1

Where can the path to a cell come from?

Hint 2

Keep the best sums of the previous row.

From brute force to the pattern: All 3ⁿ paths vs an O(n²) row DP.

Spot it: The best path to a cell comes from one of the three cells above → row-by-row DP.

Why not another pattern? Trying all paths is O(3ⁿ).

Approach:

  1. prev = first row.
  2. Each next row: cur[c] = matrix[r][c] + min(prev[c − 1], prev[c], prev[c + 1]) (within bounds).
  3. Answer: min(prev) after the last row.
class Solution:
    def minFallingPathSum(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(matrix)
        prev = matrix[0][:]  # best path sum ending at each cell of the previous row
        for r in range(1, n):
            cur = [0] * n
            for c in range(n):
                above = prev[max(0, c - 1):c + 2]  # up-left, up, up-right
                cur[c] = matrix[r][c] + min(above)
            prev = cur
        return min(prev)
function minFallingPathSum(matrix: number[][]): number {
    const n = matrix.length;
    let prev = [...matrix[0]];  // best path sum ending at each cell of the previous row
    for (let r = 1; r < n; r++) {
        const cur: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);
        for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            const above = prev.slice(Math.max(0, c - 1), c + 2);  // up-left, up, up-right
            cur[c] = matrix[r][c] + Math.min(...above);
        }
        prev = cur;
    }
    return Math.min(...prev);
}
class Solution {
    public int minFallingPathSum(int[][] matrix) {
        int n = matrix.length;
        int[] prev = matrix[0].clone();  // best path sum ending at each cell of the previous row
        for (int r = 1; r < n; r++) {
            int[] cur = new int[n];
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                int above = prev[c];  // up-left, up, up-right
                if (c > 0) {
                    above = Math.min(above, prev[c - 1]);
                }
                if (c + 1 < n) {
                    above = Math.min(above, prev[c + 1]);
                }
                cur[c] = matrix[r][c] + above;
            }
            prev = cur;
        }
        return Arrays.stream(prev).min().getAsInt();
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The slice prev[max(0, c − 1):c + 2] handles both edges.
  2. Only the previous row is needed.

  • Negative values.
  • Edge columns (two parents).

Complexity: O(n²) time, O(n) space.

On day 31, you bought a 1-day pass for costs[0] = $2 which covered day 31. In total, you spent $17 and covered all the days of your travel.

Constraints: 1 ≤ days.length ≤ 365 · 1 ≤ days[i] ≤ 365 · days is in strictly increasing order. · costs.length == 3 · 1 ≤ costs[i] ≤ 1000

Hint 1

Think about the pass that covers the last travel day.

Hint 2

dp[d] = minimum cost to cover all travel days up to day d.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every combination of passes is exponential; the day DP is O(365).

Spot it: The cheapest cover for days 1..d ends with a pass that covers day d → 1D DP over calendar days.

Why not another pattern? Greedy (buy a 7-day pass when many trips are close) misjudges overlaps; the DP checks all three choices.

Approach:

  1. cost[0] = 0.
  2. Day d not a travel day: cost[d] = cost[d − 1].
  3. Otherwise: min(cost[d−1] + c1, cost[max(0, d−7)] + c7, cost[max(0, d−30)] + c30).
class Solution:
    def mincostTickets(self, days: List[int], costs: List[int]) -> int:
        travel = set(days)
        last = days[-1]
        cost = [0] * (last + 1)  # cost[d]: cheapest way to cover travel days up to d
        for d in range(1, last + 1):
            if d not in travel:
                cost[d] = cost[d - 1]  # nothing to cover today
                continue
            cost[d] = min(cost[d - 1] + costs[0],  # 1-day pass for today
                          cost[max(0, d - 7)] + costs[1],  # 7-day pass ending today
                          cost[max(0, d - 30)] + costs[2])  # 30-day pass ending today
        return cost[last]
function mincostTickets(days: number[], costs: number[]): number {
    const travel = new Set(days);
    const last = days[days.length - 1];
    const cost: number[] = new Array(last + 1).fill(0);  // cost[d]: cheapest way to cover travel days up to d
    for (let d = 1; d <= last; d++) {
        if (!travel.has(d)) {
            cost[d] = cost[d - 1];  // nothing to cover today
            continue;
        }
        cost[d] = Math.min(
            cost[d - 1] + costs[0],                // 1-day pass for today
            cost[Math.max(0, d - 7)] + costs[1],   // 7-day pass ending today
            cost[Math.max(0, d - 30)] + costs[2],  // 30-day pass ending today
        );
    }
    return cost[last];
}
class Solution {
    public int mincostTickets(int[] days, int[] costs) {
        Set<Integer> travel = new HashSet<>();
        for (int d : days) {
            travel.add(d);
        }
        int last = days[days.length - 1];
        int[] cost = new int[last + 1];  // cost[d]: cheapest way to cover travel days up to d
        for (int d = 1; d <= last; d++) {
            if (!travel.contains(d)) {
                cost[d] = cost[d - 1];  // nothing to cover today
                continue;
            }
            cost[d] = Math.min(cost[d - 1] + costs[0],                // 1-day pass for today
                      Math.min(cost[Math.max(0, d - 7)] + costs[1],   // 7-day pass ending today
                               cost[Math.max(0, d - 30)] + costs[2]));  // 30-day pass ending today
        }
        return cost[last];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A pass bought to cover day d can be assumed to end on day d, covering the days before it.
  2. Non-travel days cost nothing extra.

  • A 7-day pass cheaper than a 1-day pass.
  • One travel day.
  • Travel every day for a month.

Complexity: O(last day) time and space (≤ 365).

Medium 1043. Partition Array for Maximum Sum Google Array

Problem: Split the array into blocks of length ≤ k; each block becomes its maximum. Return the largest possible sum.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: arr = [1,15,7,9,2,5,10], k = 3
Output: 84
Explanation: arr becomes [15,15,15,9,10,10,10]
Example 2
Input: arr = [1,4,1,5,7,3,6,1,9,9,3], k = 4
Output: 83

Constraints: 1 ≤ arr.length ≤ 500 · 0 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ k ≤ arr.length

Hint 1

Consider the last block of the partition.

Hint 2

dp[i] = best for the first i elements; try every last-block length.

From brute force to the pattern: All partitions: O(2ⁿ). DP: O(nk).

Spot it: The last block of the prefix arr[:i] has length 1..k → 1D DP over prefixes, tracking the block max while extending it leftwards.

Why not another pattern? Greedy blocks around big values can be wrong; all splits are O(2ⁿ).

Approach:

  1. best[0] = 0.
  2. For i = 1..n: for L = 1..min(k, i): top = max(top, arr[i − L]); best[i] = max(best[i], best[i − L] + top · L).
class Solution:
    def maxSumAfterPartitioning(self, arr: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        n = len(arr)
        best = [0] * (n + 1)  # best[i]: answer for arr[:i]
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            top = 0
            for L in range(1, min(k, i) + 1):  # the last block is arr[i-L:i]
                top = max(top, arr[i - L])
                best[i] = max(best[i], best[i - L] + top * L)
        return best[n]
function maxSumAfterPartitioning(arr: number[], k: number): number {
    const n = arr.length;
    const best: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(0);  // best[i]: answer for the first i elements
    for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        let top = 0;
        for (let L = 1; L <= Math.min(k, i); L++) {  // the last block is arr[i-L .. i-1]
            top = Math.max(top, arr[i - L]);
            best[i] = Math.max(best[i], best[i - L] + top * L);
        }
    }
    return best[n];
}
class Solution {
    public int maxSumAfterPartitioning(int[] arr, int k) {
        int n = arr.length;
        int[] best = new int[n + 1];  // best[i]: answer for the first i elements
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            int top = 0;
            for (int L = 1; L <= Math.min(k, i); L++) {  // the last block is arr[i-L .. i-1]
                top = Math.max(top, arr[i - L]);
                best[i] = Math.max(best[i], best[i - L] + top * L);
            }
        }
        return best[n];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Growing the last block one element to the left updates its maximum in O(1).
  2. Every block of the last partition is considered, so the best is found.

  • k = 1 → the sum.
  • k = n → n · max.
  • One element.

Complexity: O(n · k) time, O(n) space.

Medium 1048. Longest String Chain Google StringHash Map

Problem: A word is a predecessor of another if inserting one letter makes it. Return the longest chain length.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: words = ["a","b","ba","bca","bda","bdca"]
Output: 4
Explanation: One of the longest word chains is ["a","ba","bda","bdca"].
Example 2
Input: words = ["xbc","pcxbcf","xb","cxbc","pcxbc"]
Output: 5
Explanation: All the words can be put in a word chain ["xb", "xbc", "cxbc", "pcxbc", "pcxbcf"].

Constraints: 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 1000 · 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 16 · words[i] only consists of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

Process words from shortest to longest.

Hint 2

Generate predecessors by deleting one letter and look them up.

From brute force to the pattern: Comparing every pair of words is O(n² · L); generating deletions is O(n · L²).

Spot it: Chains grow by one letter, so process words by length. A word's best chain is 1 + the best among the words obtained by deleting one letter → DP with a hash map.

Why not another pattern? Checking every pair of words for the predecessor relation is O(n² · L).

Approach:

  1. Sort words by length.
  2. For each word, try deleting each position; chain[word] = max(chain.get(shorter, 0) + 1).
  3. Return the max chain.
class Solution:
    def longestStrChain(self, words: List[str]) -> int:
        chain = {}  # word -> longest chain ending with it
        for w in sorted(words, key=len):  # shorter words first
            best = 1
            for i in range(len(w)):
                shorter = w[:i] + w[i + 1:]  # delete one letter
                if shorter in chain:
                    best = max(best, chain[shorter] + 1)
            chain[w] = best
        return max(chain.values())
function longestStrChain(words: string[]): number {
    const chain = new Map<string, number>();  // word -> longest chain ending with it
    for (const w of [...words].sort((a, b) => a.length - b.length)) {  // shorter words first
        let best = 1;
        for (let i = 0; i < w.length; i++) {
            const shorter = w.slice(0, i) + w.slice(i + 1);  // delete one letter
            if (chain.has(shorter)) {
                best = Math.max(best, chain.get(shorter)! + 1);
            }
        }
        chain.set(w, best);
    }
    return Math.max(...chain.values());
}
class Solution {
    public int longestStrChain(String[] words) {
        Map<String, Integer> chain = new HashMap<>();  // word -> longest chain ending with it
        String[] sorted = words.clone();
        Arrays.sort(sorted, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length()));  // shorter words first
        int answer = 0;
        for (String w : sorted) {
            int best = 1;
            for (int i = 0; i < w.length(); i++) {
                String shorter = w.substring(0, i) + w.substring(i + 1);  // delete one letter
                if (chain.containsKey(shorter)) {
                    best = Math.max(best, chain.get(shorter) + 1);
                }
            }
            chain.put(w, best);
            answer = Math.max(answer, best);
        }
        return answer;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Deleting letters from the longer word generates its only possible predecessors (L of them).
  2. Sorting by length guarantees predecessors are already processed.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Duplicate words.
  • No chains → 1.
  • Several chains of the same length.

Complexity: O(n · L²) time (L deletions, each O(L)), O(n · L) space.

Medium 1049. Last Stone Weight II Google ArrayHash Set

Problem: Smashing stones x ≤ y leaves y − x. Return the smallest possible final weight.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: stones = [2,7,4,1,8,1]
Output: 1
Explanation: We can combine 2 and 4 to get 2, so the array converts to [2,7,1,8,1] then, we can combine 7 and 8 to get 1, so the array converts to [2,1,1,1] then, we can combine 2 and 1 to get 1, so the array converts to [1,1,1] then, we can combine 1 and 1 to get 0, so the array converts to [1], then that's the optimal value.
Example 2
Input: stones = [31,26,33,21,40]
Output: 5

Constraints: 1 ≤ stones.length ≤ 30 · 1 ≤ stones[i] ≤ 100

Hint 1

What final values are possible? Think of assigning a + or − sign to each stone.

Hint 2

Find a subset whose sum is as close as possible to half the total.

From brute force to the pattern: All sign assignments: O(2ⁿ). Subset sums: O(n · total).

Spot it: Every final result is |sum(A) − sum(B)| for some split into two groups (signs + and −). Minimise it by finding the subset sum closest to total / 2 → subset-sum DP.

Why not another pattern? Simulating smashes greedily (largest two) is the easier problem 1046 and isn't optimal here.

Approach:

  1. sums = {0}; for each stone, add s + stone for every reachable s ≤ total / 2.
  2. Answer: total − 2 · max(sums).
class Solution:
    def lastStoneWeightII(self, stones: List[int]) -> int:
        total = sum(stones)
        sums = {0}  # subset sums reachable so far (only up to half the total)
        for x in stones:
            sums |= {s + x for s in sums if s + x <= total // 2}
        return total - 2 * max(sums)  # the two groups as even as possible
function lastStoneWeightII(stones: number[]): number {
    const total = stones.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    const sums = new Set<number>([0]);  // subset sums reachable so far (only up to half the total)
    for (const x of stones) {
        for (const s of [...sums]) {
            if (s + x <= Math.floor(total / 2)) {
                sums.add(s + x);
            }
        }
    }
    return total - 2 * Math.max(...sums);  // the two groups as even as possible
}
class Solution {
    public int lastStoneWeightII(int[] stones) {
        int total = Arrays.stream(stones).sum();
        Set<Integer> sums = new HashSet<>(Set.of(0));  // subset sums reachable so far (only up to half the total)
        for (int x : stones) {
            for (int s : new ArrayList<>(sums)) {
                if (s + x <= total / 2) {
                    sums.add(s + x);
                }
            }
        }
        return total - 2 * Collections.max(sums);  // the two groups as even as possible
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each smash subtracts one group from another, so the end weight is a signed sum of the stones.
  2. The best split has one group as close to total / 2 as possible from below.
