Spot it: Grid paths with a small budget of special moves → 3D DP: (row, col, neutralisations used).

Why not another pattern? Choosing which robbers to neutralise after picking a path isn't possible without knowing the path; the budget must be part of the state.

Approach:

  1. dp[r][c][k] = best total at (r, c) having used k neutralisations.
  2. From up/left with the same k: add the cell value; if negative and k > 0, also from k − 1 adding 0.
  3. Answer max(dp[end][k]).
class Solution:
    def maximumAmount(self, coins: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        m, n = len(coins), len(coins[0])
        NEG = float("-inf")
        dp = [[[NEG] * 3 for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(m)]  # dp[r][c][k]: k robbers neutralised
        for r in range(m):
            for c in range(n):
                x = coins[r][c]
                for k in range(3):
                    if r == 0 and c == 0:
                        best_before = 0 if k == 0 else NEG
                        prev_k1 = 0 if k == 1 else NEG
                    else:
                        best_before = max(dp[r - 1][c][k] if r else NEG, dp[r][c - 1][k] if c else NEG)
                        prev_k1 = max(dp[r - 1][c][k - 1] if r and k else NEG, dp[r][c - 1][k - 1] if c and k else NEG)
                    take = best_before + x  # keep this cell as is
                    skip = prev_k1 if x < 0 else NEG  # neutralise this robber
                    dp[r][c][k] = max(take, skip)
        return max(dp[m - 1][n - 1])
function maximumAmount(coins: number[][]): number {
    const m = coins.length, n = coins[0].length;
    const NEG = -Infinity;
    // dp[r][c][k]: k robbers neutralised
    const dp: number[][][] = Array.from({ length: m }, () => Array.from({ length: n }, () => [NEG, NEG, NEG]));
    for (let r = 0; r < m; r++) {
        for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            const x = coins[r][c];
            for (let k = 0; k < 3; k++) {
                let bestBefore: number, prevK1: number;
                if (r === 0 && c === 0) {
                    bestBefore = k === 0 ? 0 : NEG;
                    prevK1 = k === 1 ? 0 : NEG;
                } else {
                    bestBefore = Math.max(r ? dp[r - 1][c][k] : NEG, c ? dp[r][c - 1][k] : NEG);
                    prevK1 = Math.max(r && k ? dp[r - 1][c][k - 1] : NEG, c && k ? dp[r][c - 1][k - 1] : NEG);
                }
                const take = bestBefore + x;  // keep this cell as is
                const skip = x < 0 ? prevK1 : NEG;  // neutralise this robber
                dp[r][c][k] = Math.max(take, skip);
            }
        }
    }
    return Math.max(...dp[m - 1][n - 1]);
}
class Solution {
    public int maximumAmount(int[][] coins) {
        int m = coins.length, n = coins[0].length;
        final int NEG = Integer.MIN_VALUE / 2;  // "impossible", with room to add a coin
        int[][][] dp = new int[m][n][3];  // dp[r][c][k]: k robbers neutralised
        for (int r = 0; r < m; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                int x = coins[r][c];
                for (int k = 0; k < 3; k++) {
                    int bestBefore, prevK1;
                    if (r == 0 && c == 0) {
                        bestBefore = k == 0 ? 0 : NEG;
                        prevK1 = k == 1 ? 0 : NEG;
                    } else {
                        bestBefore = Math.max(r > 0 ? dp[r - 1][c][k] : NEG, c > 0 ? dp[r][c - 1][k] : NEG);
                        prevK1 = Math.max(r > 0 && k > 0 ? dp[r - 1][c][k - 1] : NEG, c > 0 && k > 0 ? dp[r][c - 1][k - 1] : NEG);
                    }
                    int take = bestBefore + x;  // keep this cell as is
                    int skip = x < 0 ? prevK1 : NEG;  // neutralise this robber
                    dp[r][c][k] = Math.max(take, skip);
                }
            }
        }
        return Math.max(dp[m - 1][n - 1][0], Math.max(dp[m - 1][n - 1][1], dp[m - 1][n - 1][2]));
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. k counts robbers neutralised so far; neutralising this cell moves from k − 1 to k and adds 0.
  2. The start cell can also be a robber, hence the special case.
  3. Neutralising is only offered on negative cells.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Robber at the start or end.
  • No robbers (plain max path).
  • More than two robbers.

Complexity: O(m · n · 3) time and space.

Medium 3434. Maximum Frequency After Subarray Operation Amazon Array

Problem: Add one value x to every element of a chosen subarray once. Return the maximum possible frequency of k.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,4,5,6], k = 1
Output: 2
Explanation: After adding -5 to nums[2..5], 1 has a frequency of 2 in [1, 2, -2, -1, 0, 1].
Example 2
Input: nums = [10,2,3,4,5,5,4,3,2,2], k = 10
Output: 4
Explanation: After adding 8 to nums[1..9], 10 has a frequency of 4 in [10, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 12, 11, 10, 10].

Constraints: 1 ≤ n == nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 50 · 1 ≤ k ≤ 50

Hint 1

Which values can become k after one +x on a subarray?

Hint 2

For a fixed value v, the gain on a subarray is (#v) − (#k): maximum subarray.

From brute force to the pattern: All subarrays and shifts: O(50 n²); Kadane per value: O(50 n).

Spot it: Choosing x = k − v turns every v in the subarray into k, but breaks the ks already there. For each v, the best subarray maximises #v − #k → Kadane's maximum subarray. Values are ≤ 50, so try each v.

Why not another pattern? All subarrays × all x is O(n² · 50).

Approach:

  1. base = count(k).
  2. For each value v ≠ k: Kadane over +1 (v), −1 (k), 0 otherwise; best ≥ 0.
  3. Answer base + max gain.
class Solution:
    def maxFrequency(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        base = nums.count(k)
        best_gain = 0
        for v in set(nums):
            if v == k:
                continue
            cur = 0
            for x in nums:
                if x == v:
                    cur += 1  # becomes k
                elif x == k:
                    cur -= 1  # stops being k
                cur = max(cur, 0)  # start over if negative
                best_gain = max(best_gain, cur)
        return base + best_gain
function maxFrequency(nums: number[], k: number): number {
    const base = nums.filter((x) => x === k).length;
    let bestGain = 0;
    for (const v of new Set(nums)) {
        if (v === k) {
            continue;
        }
        let cur = 0;
        for (const x of nums) {
            if (x === v) {
                cur += 1;  // becomes k
            } else if (x === k) {
                cur -= 1;  // stops being k
            }
            cur = Math.max(cur, 0);  // start over if negative
            bestGain = Math.max(bestGain, cur);
        }
    }
    return base + bestGain;
}
class Solution {
    public int maxFrequency(int[] nums, int k) {
        int base = 0;
        Set<Integer> values = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : nums) {
            if (x == k) {
                base++;
            }
            values.add(x);
        }
        int bestGain = 0;
        for (int v : values) {
            if (v == k) {
                continue;
            }
            int cur = 0;
            for (int x : nums) {
                if (x == v) {
                    cur += 1;  // becomes k
                } else if (x == k) {
                    cur -= 1;  // stops being k
                }
                cur = Math.max(cur, 0);  // start over if negative
                bestGain = Math.max(bestGain, cur);
            }
        }
        return base + bestGain;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Inside the subarray only one value can be turned into k (one fixed x).
  2. Kadane finds the subarray where the gain #v − #k is largest.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already all k.
  • No k present.
  • Several candidate values.

Complexity: O(50 · n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 3857. Minimum Cost to Split into Ones Amazon Math

Problem: Splitting x into a + b costs a · b. Return the minimum total cost to split n into n ones.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 3
Output: 3
Explanation: One optimal set of operations is: x a b a + b a * b Cost 3 1 2 3 2 2 2 1 1 2 1 1 Thus, the minimum total cost is 2 + 1 = 3.
Example 2
Input: n = 4
Output: 6
Explanation: One optimal set of operations is: x a b a + b a * b Cost 4 2 2 4 4 4 2 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 1 2 1 1 Thus, the minimum total cost is 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 500

Hint 1

Try small n by hand. Does the order of splits matter?

Hint 2

Think of the n units as people; what does each split's cost count?

From brute force to the pattern: The DP is O(n²); the counting argument gives O(1).

Spot it: The natural formulation is a DP: dp[x] = min(a · (x − a) + dp[a] + dp[x − a]). Working it out shows every split order costs the same: each pair of the final ones is "separated" exactly once, so the total is n(n − 1)/2.

Why not another pattern? Nothing smarter than the formula is needed once you see the invariant; the DP confirms it.

Approach:

  1. Return n · (n − 1) / 2 (the DP gives the same value).
class Solution:
    def minCost(self, n: int) -> int:
        dp = [0] * (n + 1)  # dp[x]: cost to split x into ones
        for x in range(2, n + 1):
            dp[x] = min(a * (x - a) + dp[a] + dp[x - a] for a in range(1, x // 2 + 1))
        return dp[n]  # always x * (x - 1) // 2
function minCost(n: number): number {
    const dp: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(0);  // dp[x]: cost to split x into ones
    for (let x = 2; x <= n; x++) {
        let best = Infinity;
        for (let a = 1; a <= Math.floor(x / 2); a++) {
            best = Math.min(best, a * (x - a) + dp[a] + dp[x - a]);
        }
        dp[x] = best;
    }
    return dp[n];  // always x * (x - 1) / 2
}
class Solution {
    public int minCost(int n) {
        int[] dp = new int[n + 1];  // dp[x]: cost to split x into ones
        for (int x = 2; x <= n; x++) {
            int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
            for (int a = 1; a <= x / 2; a++) {
                best = Math.min(best, a * (x - a) + dp[a] + dp[x - a]);
            }
            dp[x] = best;
        }
        return dp[n];  // always x * (x - 1) / 2
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Splitting a + b costs a · b, the number of pairs with one unit on each side.
  2. Every pair of units is separated by exactly one split, so the total is the number of pairs n(n − 1)/2.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • n = 1 → 0.
  • n = 2 → 1.
  • Large n.

Complexity: O(n²) for the DP (O(1) with the formula).

Hard 472. Concatenated Words Amazon StringHash Set

Problem: Return every word that is a concatenation of at least two other words from the list (any order).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: words = ["cat","cats","catsdogcats","dog","dogcatsdog","hippopotamuses","rat","ratcatdogcat"]
Output: ["catsdogcats","dogcatsdog","ratcatdogcat"]
Explanation: "catsdogcats" can be concatenated by "cats", "dog" and "cats"; "dogcatsdog" can be concatenated by "dog", "cats" and "dog"; "ratcatdogcat" can be concatenated by "rat", "cat", "dog" and "cat".
Example 2
Input: words = ["cat","dog","catdog"]
Output: ["catdog"]

Constraints: 1 ≤ words.length ≤ 10⁴ · 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 30 · words[i] consists of only lowercase English letters. · All the strings of words are unique. · 1 ≤ sum(words[i].length) ≤ 10⁵

Hint 1

Which words can be pieces of a given word?

Hint 2

Sort by length and run Word Break against the shorter words.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying combinations of words is exponential; per-word DP is polynomial.

Spot it: A word can only be built from shorter words. Process words by length and run Word Break's DP against the set of shorter words; add each word to the set afterwards.

Why not another pattern? Checking every pair or triple of words is exponential in the number of pieces.

Approach:

  1. Sort words by length; known = set().
  2. For each word: ok[0] = True; ok[j] = any(ok[i] and word[i:j] in known).
  3. If ok[len], it's concatenated. Add the word to known.
class Solution:
    def findAllConcatenatedWordsInADict(self, words: List[str]) -> List[str]:
        known = set()
        result = []
        for word in sorted(words, key=len):  # pieces are always shorter
            if word:
                ok = [True] + [False] * len(word)  # ok[j]: word[:j] splits into known words
                for j in range(1, len(word) + 1):
                    for i in range(j):
                        if ok[i] and word[i:j] in known:
                            ok[j] = True
                            break
                if ok[-1]:
                    result.append(word)  # built from at least two shorter words
            known.add(word)
        return result
function findAllConcatenatedWordsInADict(words: string[]): string[] {
    const known = new Set<string>();
    const result: string[] = [];
    for (const word of [...words].sort((a, b) => a.length - b.length)) {  // pieces are always shorter
        if (word) {
            const ok: boolean[] = [true, ...new Array(word.length).fill(false)];  // ok[j]: word.slice(0, j) splits into known words
            for (let j = 1; j <= word.length; j++) {
                for (let i = 0; i < j; i++) {
                    if (ok[i] && known.has(word.slice(i, j))) {
                        ok[j] = true;
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
            if (ok[word.length]) {
                result.push(word);  // built from at least two shorter words
            }
        }
        known.add(word);
    }
    return result;
}
class Solution {
    public List<String> findAllConcatenatedWordsInADict(String[] words) {
        Set<String> known = new HashSet<>();
        List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
        String[] sorted = words.clone();
        Arrays.sort(sorted, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length()));  // pieces are always shorter
        for (String word : sorted) {
            if (!word.isEmpty()) {
                boolean[] ok = new boolean[word.length() + 1];  // ok[j]: word.substring(0, j) splits into known words
                ok[0] = true;
                for (int j = 1; j <= word.length(); j++) {
                    for (int i = 0; i < j; i++) {
                        if (ok[i] && known.contains(word.substring(i, j))) {
                            ok[j] = true;
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                }
                if (ok[word.length()]) {
                    result.add(word);  // built from at least two shorter words
                }
            }
            known.add(word);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Because known holds only shorter words, a successful split always uses at least two pieces.
  2. It's the Word Break DP per word.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Empty string in the list.
  • Words built from repeated pieces (catcat).
  • No concatenated words.

Complexity: O(Σ L³) worst case (slicing), usually much faster.

Hard 689. Maximum Sum of 3 Non-Overlapping Subarrays Amazon Array

Problem: Pick three non-overlapping subarrays of length k with the maximum total; return their start indices (lexicographically smallest on ties).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,1,2,6,7,5,1], k = 2
Output: [0,3,5]
Explanation: Subarrays [1, 2], [2, 6], [7, 5] correspond to the starting indices [0, 3, 5]. We could have also taken [2, 1], but an answer of [1, 3, 5] would be lexicographically larger.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,1,2,1,2,1,2,1], k = 2
Output: [0,2,4]

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 2 * 10⁴ · 1 ≤ nums[i] < 2¹⁶ · 1 ≤ k ≤ floor(nums.length / 3)

Hint 1

Precompute all window sums.

Hint 2

Fix the middle window; what are the best choices for the other two?

From brute force to the pattern: All triples: O(n³); prefix/suffix best indices: O(n).

Spot it: Compute every window sum (sliding window / prefix sums). For each middle window, the best left window must end before it and the best right one start after it: prefix and suffix DP of the best window index.

Why not another pattern? Trying all triples of windows is O(n³).

Approach:

  1. W[i] = sum of nums[i..i+k−1].
  2. left[i] = index of the best window in [0, i] (earliest on ties); right[i] = best in [i, end] (earliest on ties).
  3. For middle j: total W[left[j−k]] + W[j] + W[right[j+k]].
class Solution:
    def maxSumOfThreeSubarrays(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
        n = len(nums)
        W = [sum(nums[:k])]
        for i in range(k, n):
            W.append(W[-1] + nums[i] - nums[i - k])  # window sums
        m = len(W)
        left = [0] * m  # left[i]: best window start in [0, i]
        for i in range(1, m):
            left[i] = i if W[i] > W[left[i - 1]] else left[i - 1]  # strict: keep the earliest
        right = [m - 1] * m  # right[i]: best window start in [i, m - 1]
        for i in range(m - 2, -1, -1):
            right[i] = i if W[i] >= W[right[i + 1]] else right[i + 1]  # >=: prefer the earlier one
        best = None
        for j in range(k, m - k):  # middle window
            a, c = left[j - k], right[j + k]
            total = W[a] + W[j] + W[c]
            if best is None or total > best[0]:
                best = (total, [a, j, c])
        return best[1]
function maxSumOfThreeSubarrays(nums: number[], k: number): number[] {
    const n = nums.length;
    const W: number[] = [nums.slice(0, k).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)];
    for (let i = k; i < n; i++) {
        W.push(W[W.length - 1] + nums[i] - nums[i - k]);  // window sums
    }
    const m = W.length;
    const left: number[] = new Array(m).fill(0);  // left[i]: best window start in [0, i]
    for (let i = 1; i < m; i++) {
        left[i] = W[i] > W[left[i - 1]] ? i : left[i - 1];  // strict: keep the earliest
    }
    const right: number[] = new Array(m).fill(m - 1);  // right[i]: best window start in [i, m - 1]
    for (let i = m - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
        right[i] = W[i] >= W[right[i + 1]] ? i : right[i + 1];  // >=: prefer the earlier one
    }
    let best: [number, number[]] | null = null;
    for (let j = k; j < m - k; j++) {  // middle window
        const a = left[j - k], c = right[j + k];
        const total = W[a] + W[j] + W[c];
        if (best === null || total > best[0]) {
            best = [total, [a, j, c]];
        }
    }
    return best![1];
}
class Solution {
    public int[] maxSumOfThreeSubarrays(int[] nums, int k) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int m = n - k + 1;
        int[] W = new int[m];  // window sums
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
            W[0] += nums[i];
        }
        for (int i = k; i < n; i++) {
            W[i - k + 1] = W[i - k] + nums[i] - nums[i - k];
        }
        int[] left = new int[m];  // left[i]: best window start in [0, i]
        for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) {
            left[i] = W[i] > W[left[i - 1]] ? i : left[i - 1];  // strict: keep the earliest
        }
        int[] right = new int[m];  // right[i]: best window start in [i, m - 1]
        right[m - 1] = m - 1;
        for (int i = m - 2; i >= 0; i--) {
            right[i] = W[i] >= W[right[i + 1]] ? i : right[i + 1];  // >=: prefer the earlier one
        }
        int[] best = null;
        long bestTotal = Long.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int j = k; j < m - k; j++) {  // middle window
            int a = left[j - k], c = right[j + k];
            long total = (long) W[a] + W[j] + W[c];
            if (best == null || total > bestTotal) {
                bestTotal = total;
                best = new int[] {a, j, c};
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. left and right are prefix/suffix maxima of window sums, storing indices.
  2. Tie rules (strict on the left, ≥ on the right, strict for the middle) give the lexicographically smallest answer.
  3. The middle window leaves room for a full window on each side.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Ties (earliest indices).
  • n = 3k (only one choice).
  • Equal values everywhere.

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Hard 805. Split Array With Same Average Amazon Array

Problem: Split nums into two non-empty parts with the same average.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]
Output: true
Explanation: We can split the array into [1,4,5,8] and [2,3,6,7], and both of them have an average of 4.5.
Example 2
Input: nums = [3,1]
Output: false

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 30 · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

If both parts have the same average, what is that average?

Hint 2

For a part of size k, what must its sum be?

Hint 3

Subset-sum DP over (size, sum).

From brute force to the pattern: All subsets: 2ⁿ; meet in the middle: 2^(n/2); size-indexed bitsets: polynomial in n and the sum.

Spot it: Both parts have the overall average, so a subset A of size k must sum to total · k / n. That's a subset-sum DP indexed by size; Python integers as bitsets make each size's reachable sums one shift-or per number.

Why not another pattern? Trying all 2ⁿ subsets is 10⁹ for n = 30.

Approach:

  1. reach[k] = bitset of sums of size-k subsets; reach[0] = 1.
  2. For each number x, for k downwards: reach[k + 1] |= reach[k] << x.
  3. Check any 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2 with total·k % n == 0 and that bit set.
class Solution:
    def splitArraySameAverage(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        n, total = len(nums), sum(nums)
        half = n // 2
        if not any(total * k % n == 0 for k in range(1, half + 1)):
            return False  # no subset size can have an integer target sum
        reach = [0] * (half + 1)  # reach[k]: bit s set if some k numbers sum to s
        reach[0] = 1
        for x in nums:
            for k in range(half - 1, -1, -1):  # downwards: each number used once
                reach[k + 1] |= reach[k] << x
        return any(total * k % n == 0 and reach[k] >> (total * k // n) & 1 for k in range(1, half + 1))
function splitArraySameAverage(nums: number[]): boolean {
    const n = nums.length, total = nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    const half = Math.floor(n / 2);
    let possible = false;
    for (let k = 1; k <= half; k++) {
        if ((total * k) % n === 0) {
            possible = true;
        }
    }
    if (!possible) {
        return false;  // no subset size can have an integer target sum
    }
    const reach: bigint[] = new Array(half + 1).fill(0n);  // reach[k]: bit s set if some k numbers sum to s
    reach[0] = 1n;
    for (const x of nums) {
        for (let k = half - 1; k >= 0; k--) {  // downwards: each number used once
            reach[k + 1] |= reach[k] << BigInt(x);
        }
    }
    for (let k = 1; k <= half; k++) {
        if ((total * k) % n === 0 && ((reach[k] >> BigInt((total * k) / n)) & 1n)) {
            return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}
import java.math.BigInteger;

class Solution {
    public boolean splitArraySameAverage(int[] nums) {
        int n = nums.length, total = Arrays.stream(nums).sum();
        int half = n / 2;
        boolean possible = false;
        for (int k = 1; k <= half; k++) {
            if (total * k % n == 0) {
                possible = true;
            }
        }
        if (!possible) {
            return false;  // no subset size can have an integer target sum
        }
        BigInteger[] reach = new BigInteger[half + 1];  // reach[k]: bit s set if some k numbers sum to s
        Arrays.fill(reach, BigInteger.ZERO);
        reach[0] = BigInteger.ONE;
        for (int x : nums) {
            for (int k = half - 1; k >= 0; k--) {  // downwards: each number used once
                reach[k + 1] = reach[k + 1].or(reach[k].shiftLeft(x));
            }
        }
        for (int k = 1; k <= half; k++) {
            if (total * k % n == 0 && reach[k].testBit(total * k / n)) {
                return true;
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If a part has the overall average, the other part does too.
  2. The smaller part has at most n/2 elements, so only those sizes are needed.
  3. A left shift by x adds x to every reachable sum at once.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • n = 1 → false.
  • All equal → true (n ≥ 2).
  • No integer target for any size.

Complexity: O(n² · total / w) with big-integer bit operations.

Hard 940. Distinct Subsequences II Amazon String

Problem: Count distinct non-empty subsequences of s (mod 10⁹ + 7).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "abc"
Output: 7
Explanation: The 7 distinct subsequences are "a", "b", "c", "ab", "ac", "bc", and "abc".
Example 2
Input: s = "aba"
Output: 6
Explanation: The 6 distinct subsequences are "a", "b", "ab", "aa", "ba", and "aba".

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 2000 · s consists of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

Group distinct subsequences by their last character.

Hint 2

When c appears again, what are all the distinct subsequences ending in c?

From brute force to the pattern: Enumerating subsequences is exponential; the per-letter DP is linear.

Spot it: Classify distinct subsequences by their last letter. When c appears again, every distinct subsequence so far (plus the empty one) can be extended by c, and these replace the old ones ending in c → a 26-entry DP.

Why not another pattern? Enumerating subsequences is O(2ⁿ); a plain doubling count over-counts duplicates.

Approach:

  1. ends = [0] * 26.
  2. For each c: ends[c] = sum(ends) + 1.
  3. Answer sum(ends).
class Solution:
    def distinctSubseqII(self, s: str) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        ends = [0] * 26  # distinct subsequences ending with each letter
        for ch in s:
            ends[ord(ch) - 97] = (sum(ends) + 1) % MOD  # extend everything (and the empty one) by ch
        return sum(ends) % MOD
function distinctSubseqII(s: string): number {
    const MOD = 1_000_000_007;
    const ends: number[] = new Array(26).fill(0);  // distinct subsequences ending with each letter
    const sum = (): number => ends.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    for (const ch of s) {
        ends[ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97] = (sum() + 1) % MOD;  // extend everything (and the empty one) by ch
    }
    return sum() % MOD;
}
class Solution {
    public int distinctSubseqII(String s) {
        final long MOD = 1_000_000_007;
        long[] ends = new long[26];  // distinct subsequences ending with each letter
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            long sum = 0;
            for (long e : ends) {
                sum += e;
            }
            ends[ch - 'a'] = (sum + 1) % MOD;  // extend everything (and the empty one) by ch
        }
        long sum = 0;
        for (long e : ends) {
            sum += e;
        }
        return (int) (sum % MOD);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Every subsequence ending in c so far is also counted in the new value (extend its prefix again), so overwriting avoids duplicates.
  2. The + 1 is the single letter c.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • All the same letter → n.
  • All distinct → 2ⁿ − 1.
  • Repeated patterns.

Complexity: O(26 · n) time, O(1) space.

Hard 1000. Minimum Cost to Merge Stones Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Merge exactly k consecutive piles at a time (cost = their total). Return the minimum cost to end with one pile, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: stones = [3,2,4,1], k = 2
Output: 20
Explanation: We start with [3, 2, 4, 1]. We merge [3, 2] for a cost of 5, and we are left with [5, 4, 1]. We merge [4, 1] for a cost of 5, and we are left with [5, 5]. We merge [5, 5] for a cost of 10, and we are left with [10]. The total cost was 20, and this is the minimum possible.
Example 2
Input: stones = [3,2,4,1], k = 3
Output: -1
Explanation: After any merge operation, there are 2 piles left, and we can't merge anymore. So the task is impossible.

Constraints: n == stones.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 30 · 1 ≤ stones[i] ≤ 100 · 2 ≤ k ≤ 30

Hint 1

When is it possible at all? Count how many piles each merge removes.

Hint 2

Interval DP: split so the left part becomes one pile.

Hint 3

Add the range sum when the range can collapse to one pile.

From brute force to the pattern: All merge orders are exponential; interval DP is O(n³ / k).

Spot it: Merges of consecutive piles → interval DP. A range of length L can become one pile iff (L − 1) % (k − 1) == 0. Split the range so the left part becomes one pile; when the whole range can become one pile, pay its sum once more.

Why not another pattern? Trying merge orders is exponential.

Approach:

  1. If (n − 1) % (k − 1), return −1.
  2. dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][m] + dp[m + 1][j]) over m stepping by k − 1 (left part reducible to one pile).
  3. If (j − i) % (k − 1) == 0, add sum(stones[i..j]).
class Solution:
    def mergeStones(self, stones: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        n = len(stones)
        if (n - 1) % (k - 1):
            return -1  # piles drop by k - 1 each merge
        P = [0]
        for x in stones:
            P.append(P[-1] + x)
        dp = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]  # dp[i][j]: min cost to reduce stones[i..j] as far as possible
        for length in range(k, n + 1):
            for i in range(n - length + 1):
                j = i + length - 1
                dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][m] + dp[m + 1][j] for m in range(i, j, k - 1))  # left part ends as one pile
                if (j - i) % (k - 1) == 0:
                    dp[i][j] += P[j + 1] - P[i]  # final merge of this range into one pile
        return dp[0][n - 1]
function mergeStones(stones: number[], k: number): number {
    const n = stones.length;
    if ((n - 1) % (k - 1) !== 0) {
        return -1;  // piles drop by k - 1 each merge
    }
    const P = [0];
    for (const x of stones) {
        P.push(P[P.length - 1] + x);
    }
    // dp[i][j]: min cost to reduce stones[i..j] as far as possible
    const dp: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0));
    for (let length = k; length <= n; length++) {
        for (let i = 0; i + length <= n; i++) {
            const j = i + length - 1;
            let best = Infinity;
            for (let m = i; m < j; m += k - 1) {  // left part ends as one pile
                best = Math.min(best, dp[i][m] + dp[m + 1][j]);
            }
            dp[i][j] = best;
            if ((j - i) % (k - 1) === 0) {
                dp[i][j] += P[j + 1] - P[i];  // final merge of this range into one pile
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[0][n - 1];
}
class Solution {
    public int mergeStones(int[] stones, int k) {
        int n = stones.length;
        if ((n - 1) % (k - 1) != 0) {
            return -1;  // piles drop by k - 1 each merge
        }
        int[] P = new int[n + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            P[i + 1] = P[i] + stones[i];
        }
        int[][] dp = new int[n][n];  // dp[i][j]: min cost to reduce stones[i..j] as far as possible
        for (int length = k; length <= n; length++) {
            for (int i = 0; i + length <= n; i++) {
                int j = i + length - 1;
                int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
                for (int m = i; m < j; m += k - 1) {  // left part ends as one pile
                    best = Math.min(best, dp[i][m] + dp[m + 1][j]);
                }
                dp[i][j] = best;
                if ((j - i) % (k - 1) == 0) {
                    dp[i][j] += P[j + 1] - P[i];  // final merge of this range into one pile
                }
            }
        }
        return dp[0][n - 1];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each merge reduces the pile count by k − 1, which gives the feasibility test.
  2. Stepping m by k − 1 keeps the left part reducible to exactly one pile.
  3. The last merge of a range costs its total, added once when the range can become a single pile.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Impossible → −1.
  • k = 2 (classic merge).
  • n = 1 → 0.

Complexity: O(n³ / k) time, O(n²) space.

Hard 1335. Minimum Difficulty of a Job Schedule Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Do jobs in order over exactly d days (at least one per day); a day's difficulty is its hardest job. Minimise the sum, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: jobDifficulty = [6,5,4,3,2,1], d = 2
Output: 7
Explanation: First day you can finish the first 5 jobs, total difficulty = 6. Second day you can finish the last job, total difficulty = 1. The difficulty of the schedule = 6 + 1 = 7
Example 2
Input: jobDifficulty = [9,9,9], d = 4
Output: -1
Explanation: If you finish a job per day you will still have a free day. you cannot find a schedule for the given jobs.

Constraints: 1 ≤ jobDifficulty.length ≤ 300 · 0 ≤ jobDifficulty[i] ≤ 1000 · 1 ≤ d ≤ 10

Hint 1

Think about the last day: which jobs does it cover?

Hint 2

dp over (days, jobs done), trying every start of the last day.

From brute force to the pattern: All split choices are combinatorial; the DP is O(dn²).

Spot it: Split the sequence into d contiguous parts → partition DP over (days used, jobs done), tracking the last part's maximum while extending it.

Why not another pattern? Trying all split points is C(n − 1, d − 1).

Approach:

  1. If n < d, −1.
  2. dp[k][i] = best for the first i jobs in k days.
  3. For the last day covering jobs j..i−1, extend j leftwards keeping the running max.
class Solution:
    def minDifficulty(self, jobDifficulty: List[int], d: int) -> int:
        n = len(jobDifficulty)
        if n < d:
            return -1  # each day needs a job
        INF = float("inf")
        dp = [[INF] * (n + 1) for _ in range(d + 1)]  # dp[k][i]: first i jobs in k days
        dp[0][0] = 0
        for k in range(1, d + 1):
            for i in range(k, n + 1):
                hardest = 0
                for j in range(i - 1, k - 2, -1):  # last day does jobs j..i-1
                    hardest = max(hardest, jobDifficulty[j])
                    if dp[k - 1][j] < INF:
                        dp[k][i] = min(dp[k][i], dp[k - 1][j] + hardest)
        return dp[d][n]
function minDifficulty(jobDifficulty: number[], d: number): number {
    const n = jobDifficulty.length;
    if (n < d) {
        return -1;  // each day needs a job
    }
    const INF = Infinity;
    const dp: number[][] = Array.from({ length: d + 1 }, () => new Array(n + 1).fill(INF));  // dp[k][i]: first i jobs in k days
    dp[0][0] = 0;
    for (let k = 1; k <= d; k++) {
        for (let i = k; i <= n; i++) {
            let hardest = 0;
            for (let j = i - 1; j >= k - 1; j--) {  // last day does jobs j..i-1
                hardest = Math.max(hardest, jobDifficulty[j]);
                if (dp[k - 1][j] < INF) {
                    dp[k][i] = Math.min(dp[k][i], dp[k - 1][j] + hardest);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[d][n];
}
class Solution {
    public int minDifficulty(int[] jobDifficulty, int d) {
        int n = jobDifficulty.length;
        if (n < d) {
            return -1;  // each day needs a job
        }
        final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int[][] dp = new int[d + 1][n + 1];  // dp[k][i]: first i jobs in k days
        for (int[] row : dp) {
            Arrays.fill(row, INF);
        }
        dp[0][0] = 0;
        for (int k = 1; k <= d; k++) {
            for (int i = k; i <= n; i++) {
                int hardest = 0;
                for (int j = i - 1; j >= k - 1; j--) {  // last day does jobs j..i-1
                    hardest = Math.max(hardest, jobDifficulty[j]);
                    if (dp[k - 1][j] < INF) {
                        dp[k][i] = Math.min(dp[k][i], dp[k - 1][j] + hardest);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return dp[d][n];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Extending the last day leftwards updates its maximum in O(1).
  2. The bound j ≥ k − 1 leaves at least one job for each earlier day.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • n < d → −1.
  • d = n (one job per day).
  • d = 1 (max of all).

Complexity: O(d · n²) time, O(d · n) space.

Hard 1478. Allocate Mailboxes Amazon Array

Problem: Place k mailboxes on a street to minimise the total distance from each house to its nearest mailbox.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: houses = [1,4,8,10,20], k = 3
Output: 5
Explanation: Allocate mailboxes in position 3, 9 and 20. Minimum total distance from each houses to nearest mailboxes is |3-1| + |4-3| + |9-8| + |10-9| + |20-20| = 5
Example 2
Input: houses = [2,3,5,12,18], k = 2
Output: 9
Explanation: Allocate mailboxes in position 3 and 14. Minimum total distance from each houses to nearest mailboxes is |2-3| + |3-3| + |5-3| + |12-14| + |18-14| = 9.

Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ houses.length ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ houses[i] ≤ 10⁴ · All the integers of houses are unique.

Hint 1

Sort the houses. What does the set of houses served by one mailbox look like?

Hint 2

Where should a single mailbox go for a group?

Hint 3

Partition the houses into k groups with DP.

From brute force to the pattern: Searching positions is huge; median costs + partition DP is polynomial.

Spot it: Sorted houses split into k contiguous groups, each served by a mailbox at its median. Precompute each group's cost, then partition DP over prefixes and number of boxes.

Why not another pattern? Trying mailbox positions is huge; groups are always contiguous after sorting.

Approach:

  1. Sort; cost[i][j] = Σ |h − median| for houses i..j.
  2. dp[b][j] = min over i of dp[b − 1][i] + cost[i][j − 1].
  3. Return dp[k][n].
class Solution:
    def minDistance(self, houses: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        h = sorted(houses)
        n = len(h)
        cost = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]  # one mailbox at the median of h[i..j]
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i, n):
                mid = h[(i + j) // 2]
                cost[i][j] = sum(abs(h[t] - mid) for t in range(i, j + 1))
        INF = float("inf")
        dp = [[INF] * (n + 1) for _ in range(k + 1)]  # dp[b][j]: first j houses with b mailboxes
        dp[0][0] = 0
        for b in range(1, k + 1):
            for j in range(1, n + 1):
                for i in range(j):  # last group is houses i..j-1
                    if dp[b - 1][i] < INF:
                        dp[b][j] = min(dp[b][j], dp[b - 1][i] + cost[i][j - 1])
        return dp[k][n]
function minDistance(houses: number[], k: number): number {
    const h = [...houses].sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const n = h.length;
    const cost: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0));  // one mailbox at the median of h[i..j]
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (let j = i; j < n; j++) {
            const mid = h[Math.floor((i + j) / 2)];
            for (let t = i; t <= j; t++) {
                cost[i][j] += Math.abs(h[t] - mid);
            }
        }
    }
    const INF = Infinity;
    const dp: number[][] = Array.from({ length: k + 1 }, () => new Array(n + 1).fill(INF));  // dp[b][j]: first j houses with b mailboxes
    dp[0][0] = 0;
    for (let b = 1; b <= k; b++) {
        for (let j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            for (let i = 0; i < j; i++) {  // last group is houses i..j-1
                if (dp[b - 1][i] < INF) {
                    dp[b][j] = Math.min(dp[b][j], dp[b - 1][i] + cost[i][j - 1]);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[k][n];
}
class Solution {
    public int minDistance(int[] houses, int k) {
        int[] h = houses.clone();
        Arrays.sort(h);
        int n = h.length;
        int[][] cost = new int[n][n];  // one mailbox at the median of h[i..j]
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = i; j < n; j++) {
                int mid = h[(i + j) / 2];
                for (int t = i; t <= j; t++) {
                    cost[i][j] += Math.abs(h[t] - mid);
                }
            }
        }
        final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int[][] dp = new int[k + 1][n + 1];  // dp[b][j]: first j houses with b mailboxes
        for (int[] row : dp) {
            Arrays.fill(row, INF);
        }
        dp[0][0] = 0;
        for (int b = 1; b <= k; b++) {
            for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
                for (int i = 0; i < j; i++) {  // last group is houses i..j-1
                    if (dp[b - 1][i] < INF) {
                        dp[b][j] = Math.min(dp[b][j], dp[b - 1][i] + cost[i][j - 1]);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return dp[k][n];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each mailbox serves a contiguous block of sorted houses.
  2. The median minimises the sum of distances within a block.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k equals the number of houses → 0.
  • k = 1.
  • Clustered houses.

Complexity: O(n³ + k n²) time, O(n²) space (n ≤ 100).

Hard 1494. Parallel Courses II Amazon GraphArray

Problem: With prerequisites and at most k courses per semester, return the minimum number of semesters (n ≤ 15).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 4, relations = [[2,1],[3,1],[1,4]], k = 2
Output: 3
Explanation: The figure above represents the given graph. In the first semester, you can take courses 2 and 3. In the second semester, you can take course 1. In the third semester, you can take course 4.
Example 2
Input: n = 5, relations = [[2,1],[3,1],[4,1],[1,5]], k = 2
Output: 4
Explanation: The figure above represents the given graph. In the first semester, you can only take courses 2 and 3 since you cannot take more than two per semester. In the second semester, you can take course 4. In the third semester, you can take course 1. In the fourth semester, you can take course 5.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 15 · 1 ≤ k ≤ n · 0 ≤ relations.length ≤ n * (n-1) / 2 · relations[i].length == 2 · 1 ≤ prevCoursei, nextCoursei ≤ n · prevCoursei != nextCoursei · All the pairs [prevCoursei, nextCoursei] are unique. · The given graph is a directed acyclic graph.

Hint 1

Why does a greedy topological order fail?

Hint 2

n ≤ 15: use the set of taken courses as the DP state.

Hint 3

Each semester takes a subset of the available courses.

From brute force to the pattern: Greedy is wrong; bitmask DP over submasks is O(3ⁿ) and exact.

Spot it: Greedy (take any k available) is wrong. With n ≤ 15, the state is the set of courses taken → bitmask DP; each semester picks a submask of the available courses of size ≤ k (or all of them if fewer).

Why not another pattern? Topological sort with greedy choices can pick the wrong courses and need extra semesters.

Approach:

  1. pre[i] = bitmask of prerequisites.
  2. BFS/DP over masks: available = courses not taken whose pre ⊆ mask.
  3. If popcount(available) ≤ k, take all; else try every submask of size k.
class Solution:
    def minNumberOfSemesters(self, n: int, relations: List[List[int]], k: int) -> int:
        pre = [0] * n
        for a, b in relations:
            pre[b - 1] |= 1 << (a - 1)
        full = (1 << n) - 1
        INF = float("inf")
        dp = [INF] * (1 << n)  # dp[mask]: semesters to take exactly `mask`
        dp[0] = 0
        for mask in range(1 << n):
            if dp[mask] == INF:
                continue
            avail = 0
            for i in range(n):
                if not mask >> i & 1 and pre[i] & mask == pre[i]:
                    avail |= 1 << i  # prerequisites done, not yet taken
            if bin(avail).count("1") <= k:
                dp[mask | avail] = min(dp[mask | avail], dp[mask] + 1)  # take them all
                continue
            sub = avail
            while sub:
                if bin(sub).count("1") == k:
                    dp[mask | sub] = min(dp[mask | sub], dp[mask] + 1)
                sub = (sub - 1) & avail  # next submask
        return dp[full]
function minNumberOfSemesters(n: number, relations: number[][], k: number): number {
    const pre: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);
    for (const [a, b] of relations) {
        pre[b - 1] |= 1 << (a - 1);
    }
    const full = (1 << n) - 1;
    const INF = Infinity;
    const bits = (x: number): number => x.toString(2).split("1").length - 1;
    const dp: number[] = new Array(1 << n).fill(INF);  // dp[mask]: semesters to take exactly `mask`
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (let mask = 0; mask < 1 << n; mask++) {
        if (dp[mask] === INF) {
            continue;
        }
        let avail = 0;
        for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (!((mask >> i) & 1) && (pre[i] & mask) === pre[i]) {
                avail |= 1 << i;  // prerequisites done, not yet taken
            }
        }
        if (bits(avail) <= k) {
            dp[mask | avail] = Math.min(dp[mask | avail], dp[mask] + 1);  // take them all
            continue;
        }
        let sub = avail;
        while (sub) {
            if (bits(sub) === k) {
                dp[mask | sub] = Math.min(dp[mask | sub], dp[mask] + 1);
            }
            sub = (sub - 1) & avail;  // next submask
        }
    }
    return dp[full];
}
class Solution {
    public int minNumberOfSemesters(int n, int[][] relations, int k) {
        int[] pre = new int[n];
        for (int[] r : relations) {
            pre[r[1] - 1] |= 1 << (r[0] - 1);
        }
        int full = (1 << n) - 1;
        final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int[] dp = new int[1 << n];  // dp[mask]: semesters to take exactly `mask`
        Arrays.fill(dp, INF);
        dp[0] = 0;
        for (int mask = 0; mask < 1 << n; mask++) {
            if (dp[mask] == INF) {
                continue;
            }
            int avail = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                if ((mask >> i & 1) == 0 && (pre[i] & mask) == pre[i]) {
                    avail |= 1 << i;  // prerequisites done, not yet taken
                }
            }
            if (Integer.bitCount(avail) <= k) {
                dp[mask | avail] = Math.min(dp[mask | avail], dp[mask] + 1);  // take them all
                continue;
            }
            int sub = avail;
            while (sub != 0) {
                if (Integer.bitCount(sub) == k) {
                    dp[mask | sub] = Math.min(dp[mask | sub], dp[mask] + 1);
                }
                sub = (sub - 1) & avail;  // next submask
            }
        }
        return dp[full];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Taking fewer than possible when at most k are available never helps, so all are taken.
  2. Otherwise exactly k (more is not allowed, fewer is never better).
  3. Submask enumeration (sub − 1) & avail visits every subset of the available courses.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • No relations (ceil(n / k)).
  • A long chain (n semesters).
  • k ≥ n.

Complexity: O(3ⁿ) time in the worst case, O(2ⁿ) space.

Hard 1547. Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Cutting a stick costs its current length. Make all the given cuts in the best order; return the minimum total cost.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 7, cuts = [1,3,4,5]
Output: 16
Explanation: Using cuts order = [1, 3, 4, 5] as in the input leads to the following scenario: The first cut is done to a rod of length 7 so the cost is 7. The second cut is done to a rod of length 6 (i.e. the second part of the first cut), the third is done to a rod of length 4 and the last cut is to a rod of length 3. The total cost is 7 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 20. Rearranging the cuts to be [3, 5, 1, 4] for example will lead to a scenario with total cost = 16 (as shown in the example photo 7 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 16).
Example 2
Input: n = 9, cuts = [5,6,1,4,2]
Output: 22
Explanation: If you try the given cuts ordering the cost will be 25. There are much ordering with total cost <= 25, for example, the order [4, 6, 5, 2, 1] has total cost = 22 which is the minimum possible.

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ · 1 ≤ cuts.length ≤ min(n - 1, 100) · 1 ≤ cuts[i] ≤ n - 1 · All the integers in cuts array are distinct.

Hint 1

The first cut on a piece splits it into two independent problems.

Hint 2

Define dp on pairs of cut positions.

From brute force to the pattern: All cut orders are c!; interval DP is O(c³).

Spot it: After the first cut inside (p_i, p_j) the two sides are independent → interval DP over consecutive cut points, like Burst Balloons.

Why not another pattern? Trying all cut orders is factorial.

Approach:

  1. P = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n].
  2. dp[i][j] = min cost to make every cut strictly between P[i] and P[j].
  3. dp[i][j] = P[j] − P[i] + min(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]) for i < k < j; 0 if no cut between.
class Solution:
    def minCost(self, n: int, cuts: List[int]) -> int:
        P = [0] + sorted(cuts) + [n]
        m = len(P)
        dp = [[0] * m for _ in range(m)]  # dp[i][j]: cost of all cuts between P[i] and P[j]
        for gap in range(2, m):  # need at least one cut point inside
            for i in range(m - gap):
                j = i + gap
                dp[i][j] = P[j] - P[i] + min(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] for k in range(i + 1, j))  # first cut at P[k]
        return dp[0][m - 1]
function minCost(n: number, cuts: number[]): number {
    const P = [0, ...[...cuts].sort((a, b) => a - b), n];
    const m = P.length;
    const dp: number[][] = Array.from({ length: m }, () => new Array(m).fill(0));  // dp[i][j]: cost of all cuts between P[i] and P[j]
    for (let gap = 2; gap < m; gap++) {  // need at least one cut point inside
        for (let i = 0; i + gap < m; i++) {
            const j = i + gap;
            let best = Infinity;
            for (let k = i + 1; k < j; k++) {
                best = Math.min(best, dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]);  // first cut at P[k]
            }
            dp[i][j] = P[j] - P[i] + best;
        }
    }
    return dp[0][m - 1];
}
class Solution {
    public int minCost(int n, int[] cuts) {
        int m = cuts.length + 2;
        int[] P = new int[m];
        int[] sorted = cuts.clone();
        Arrays.sort(sorted);
        for (int i = 0; i < sorted.length; i++) {
            P[i + 1] = sorted[i];
        }
        P[m - 1] = n;
        int[][] dp = new int[m][m];  // dp[i][j]: cost of all cuts between P[i] and P[j]
        for (int gap = 2; gap < m; gap++) {  // need at least one cut point inside
            for (int i = 0; i + gap < m; i++) {
                int j = i + gap;
                int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
                for (int k = i + 1; k < j; k++) {
                    best = Math.min(best, dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]);  // first cut at P[k]
                }
                dp[i][j] = P[j] - P[i] + best;
            }
        }
        return dp[0][m - 1];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Whatever the first cut inside a piece is, it costs the piece's length.
  2. Intervals are filled by increasing width so sub-intervals are ready.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • One cut.
  • Cuts at many positions.
  • Unsorted cuts.

Complexity: O(c³) time, O(c²) space for c cuts.

Hard 1691. Maximum Height by Stacking Cuboids Amazon Array

Problem: Stack cuboids (rotations allowed) where each one's width, length and height are ≤ those below. Maximise the total height.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: cuboids = [[50,45,20],[95,37,53],[45,23,12]]
Output: 190
Explanation: Cuboid 1 is placed on the bottom with the 53x37 side facing down with height 95. Cuboid 0 is placed next with the 45x20 side facing down with height 50. Cuboid 2 is placed next with the 23x12 side facing down with height 45. The total height is 95 + 50 + 45 = 190.
Example 2
Input: cuboids = [[38,25,45],[76,35,3]]
Output: 76
Explanation: You can't place any of the cuboids on the other. We choose cuboid 1 and rotate it so that the 35x3 side is facing down and its height is 76.

Constraints: n == cuboids.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ widthi, lengthi, heighti ≤ 100

Hint 1

Which side should be the height?

Hint 2

After normalising each cuboid, it's a longest-chain (LIS) problem.

From brute force to the pattern: All rotations and orders are exponential; LIS-style DP is O(n²).

Spot it: Sorting each cuboid's dimensions and using the largest as height is always optimal. Then sort the cuboids; stacking is a chain where each dimension is non-decreasing → LIS-style DP.

Why not another pattern? Trying rotations and orders is exponential.

Approach:

  1. Sort each cuboid's three numbers; sort the list.
  2. dp[i] = c[i][2] + max(dp[j]) for j < i with all three dims of j ≤ those of i.
  3. Return max(dp).
class Solution:
    def maxHeight(self, cuboids: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        boxes = sorted(sorted(c) for c in cuboids)  # each box: small, medium, large (= height)
        dp = [0] * len(boxes)  # tallest stack with box i on top
        for i, (a, b, c) in enumerate(boxes):
            dp[i] = c
            for j in range(i):
                if boxes[j][0] <= a and boxes[j][1] <= b and boxes[j][2] <= c:
                    dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + c)  # box j can sit below box i
        return max(dp)
function maxHeight(cuboids: number[][]): number {
    // each box: small, medium, large (= height); boxes in lexicographic order
    const boxes = cuboids.map((c) => [...c].sort((a, b) => a - b))
        .sort((p, q) => p[0] - q[0] || p[1] - q[1] || p[2] - q[2]);
    const dp: number[] = new Array(boxes.length).fill(0);  // tallest stack with box i on top
    boxes.forEach(([a, b, c], i) => {
        dp[i] = c;
        for (let j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (boxes[j][0] <= a && boxes[j][1] <= b && boxes[j][2] <= c) {
                dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + c);  // box j can sit below box i
            }
        }
    });
    return Math.max(...dp);
}
class Solution {
    public int maxHeight(int[][] cuboids) {
        int n = cuboids.length;
        int[][] boxes = new int[n][];  // each box: small, medium, large (= height)
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            boxes[i] = cuboids[i].clone();
            Arrays.sort(boxes[i]);
        }
        Arrays.sort(boxes, (p, q) -> p[0] != q[0] ? Integer.compare(p[0], q[0])
                : p[1] != q[1] ? Integer.compare(p[1], q[1]) : Integer.compare(p[2], q[2]));
        int[] dp = new int[n];  // tallest stack with box i on top
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int a = boxes[i][0], b = boxes[i][1], c = boxes[i][2];
            dp[i] = c;
            for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
                if (boxes[j][0] <= a && boxes[j][1] <= b && boxes[j][2] <= c) {
                    dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + c);  // box j can sit below box i
                }
            }
            best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If one cuboid fits on another in some orientation, it also fits with both sorted (a known exchange argument), and sorted gives the tallest height.
  2. After sorting the list, a box can only sit on earlier boxes.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Identical cuboids.
  • One cuboid.
  • None fit on each other.

Complexity: O(n²) time, O(n) space.

Hard 2262. Total Appeal of A String Amazon String

Problem: The appeal of a string is its number of distinct letters. Sum the appeal of all substrings.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "abbca"
Output: 28
Explanation: The following are the substrings of "abbca": - Substrings of length 1: "a", "b", "b", "c", "a" have an appeal of 1, 1, 1, 1, and 1 respectively. The sum is 5. - Substrings of length 2: "ab", "bb", "bc", "ca" have an appeal of 2, 1, 2, and 2 respectively. The sum is 7. - Substrings of length 3: "abb", "bbc", "bca" have an appeal of 2, 2, and 3 respectively. The sum is 7. - Substrings of length 4: "abbc", "bbca" have an appeal of 3 and 3 respectively. The sum is 6. - Substrings of length 5: "abbca" has an appeal of 3. The sum is 3. The total sum is 5 + 7 + 7 + 6 + 3 = 28.
Example 2
Input: s = "code"
Output: 20
Explanation: The following are the substrings of "code": - Substrings of length 1: "c", "o", "d", "e" have an appeal of 1, 1, 1, and 1 respectively. The sum is 4. - Substrings of length 2: "co", "od", "de" have an appeal of 2, 2, and 2 respectively. The sum is 6. - Substrings of length 3: "cod", "ode" have an appeal of 3 and 3 respectively. The sum is 6. - Substrings of length 4: "code" has an appeal of 4. The sum is 4. The total sum is 4 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 20.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁵ · s consists of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

Instead of computing each substring's appeal, count each character's contribution.

Hint 2

When is the character at i the first of its letter in a substring?

From brute force to the pattern: All substrings: O(n²); contribution counting: O(n).

Spot it: Count each letter once per substring by crediting its first occurrence in that substring. Occurrence i is first for substrings starting after the previous same letter and ending anywhere at or after i → a counting DP with last positions.

Why not another pattern? Computing each substring's distinct count is O(n²) or worse.

Approach:

  1. last[c] = −1.
  2. For each i: add (i − last[c]) · (n − i); set last[c] = i.
class Solution:
    def appealSum(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        last = {}  # letter -> its previous index
        total = 0
        for i, ch in enumerate(s):
            starts = i - last.get(ch, -1)  # substrings where this is the first ch
            total += starts * (n - i)  # times the possible end positions
            last[ch] = i
        return total
function appealSum(s: string): number {
    const n = s.length;
    const last = new Map<string, number>();  // letter -> its previous index
    let total = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        const ch = s[i];
        const starts = i - (last.get(ch) ?? -1);  // substrings where this is the first ch
        total += starts * (n - i);  // times the possible end positions
        last.set(ch, i);
    }
    return total;
}
class Solution {
    public long appealSum(String s) {
        int n = s.length();
        int[] last = new int[26];  // letter -> its previous index (-1 = not seen)
        Arrays.fill(last, -1);
        long total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int ch = s.charAt(i) - 'a';
            long starts = i - last[ch];  // substrings where this is the first ch
            total += starts * (n - i);  // times the possible end positions
            last[ch] = i;
        }
        return total;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A substring [l, r] counts letter c exactly once, at its first occurrence inside.
  2. That occurrence is i when last[c] < l ≤ i ≤ r.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • All the same letter.
  • All distinct.
  • Single character.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(26) space.

Hard 2272. Substring With Largest Variance Amazon String

Problem: The variance of a string is the largest difference between counts of two letters present in it. Return the largest variance over all substrings.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "aababbb"
Output: 3
Explanation: All possible variances along with their respective substrings are listed below: - Variance 0 for substrings "a", "aa", "ab", "abab", "aababb", "ba", "b", "bb", and "bbb". - Variance 1 for substrings "aab", "aba", "abb", "aabab", "ababb", "aababbb", and "bab". - Variance 2 for substrings "aaba", "ababbb", "abbb", and "babb". - Variance 3 for substring "babbb". Since the largest possible variance is 3, we return it.
Example 2
Input: s = "abcde"
Output: 0
Explanation: No letter occurs more than once in s, so the variance of every substring is 0.

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10⁴ · s consists of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

Fix which letter is most frequent and which is least.

Hint 2

Then it's a maximum-subarray problem with +1 and −1, but the window must contain the rare letter.

From brute force to the pattern: All substrings with counts: O(26 n²); Kadane per letter pair: O(26² n).

Spot it: Fix the pair: letter a should be frequent and b rare. With a → +1, b → −1, others 0, it's maximum subarray (Kadane), with the extra rule that the substring must contain at least one b.

Why not another pattern? All substrings × letter counts is O(26 n²).

Approach:

  1. For each ordered pair a ≠ b (both present):
  2. Kadane with cur, has_b, and started_with_b tracking; when cur goes negative, restart (but remember a b was just seen).
  3. Update the answer only when the window contains a b.
class Solution:
    def largestVariance(self, s: str) -> int:
        letters = set(s)
        best = 0
        for a in letters:
            for b in letters:
                if a == b:
                    continue
                cur = 0  # (#a - #b) in the current window
                has_b = False  # does the window contain a b?
                restarted_on_b = False  # a b was dropped by the last restart (can be taken back)
                for ch in s:
                    if ch == a:
                        cur += 1
                    elif ch == b:
                        has_b = True
                        if restarted_on_b and cur >= 0:
                            restarted_on_b = False  # keep the previous b instead of this one
                        else:
                            cur -= 1
                            if cur < 0:
                                cur = -1  # restart at this b
                                restarted_on_b = True
                    if has_b:
                        best = max(best, cur)
        return best
function largestVariance(s: string): number {
    const letters = new Set(s);
    let best = 0;
    for (const a of letters) {
        for (const b of letters) {
            if (a === b) {
                continue;
            }
            let cur = 0;  // (#a - #b) in the current window
            let hasB = false;  // does the window contain a b?
            let restartedOnB = false;  // a b was dropped by the last restart (can be taken back)
            for (const ch of s) {
                if (ch === a) {
                    cur += 1;
                } else if (ch === b) {
                    hasB = true;
                    if (restartedOnB && cur >= 0) {
                        restartedOnB = false;  // keep the previous b instead of this one
                    } else {
                        cur -= 1;
                        if (cur < 0) {
                            cur = -1;  // restart at this b
                            restartedOnB = true;
                        }
                    }
                }
                if (hasB) {
                    best = Math.max(best, cur);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int largestVariance(String s) {
        Set<Character> letters = new HashSet<>();
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            letters.add(ch);
        }
        int best = 0;
        for (char a : letters) {
            for (char b : letters) {
                if (a == b) {
                    continue;
                }
                int cur = 0;  // (#a - #b) in the current window
                boolean hasB = false;  // does the window contain a b?
                boolean restartedOnB = false;  // a b was dropped by the last restart (can be taken back)
                for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
                    if (ch == a) {
                        cur += 1;
                    } else if (ch == b) {
                        hasB = true;
                        if (restartedOnB && cur >= 0) {
                            restartedOnB = false;  // keep the previous b instead of this one
                        } else {
                            cur -= 1;
                            if (cur < 0) {
                                cur = -1;  // restart at this b
                                restartedOnB = true;
                            }
                        }
                    }
                    if (hasB) {
                        best = Math.max(best, cur);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. With a as +1 and b as −1, the window value is count(a) − count(b).
  2. A window must contain a b (otherwise b's count is 0 and it isn't present); the has_b flag enforces that.
  3. Restarting at a b keeps that b in the window (value −1) so later as still count with one b present.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • All one letter → 0.
  • Two letters only.
  • The rare letter at the very start.

Complexity: O(26² · n) time, O(1) space.

Hard 2742. Painting the Walls Amazon Array

Problem: A paid painter takes time[i] and costs cost[i] for wall i; a free painter paints any wall in 1 unit but only while the paid one is busy. Minimise cost to paint all walls.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: cost = [1,2,3,2], time = [1,2,3,2]
Output: 3
Explanation: The walls at index 0 and 1 will be painted by the paid painter, and it will take 3 units of time; meanwhile, the free painter will paint the walls at index 2 and 3, free of cost in 2 units of time. Thus, the total cost is 1 + 2 = 3.
Example 2
Input: cost = [2,3,4,2], time = [1,1,1,1]
Output: 4
Explanation: The walls at index 0 and 3 will be painted by the paid painter, and it will take 2 units of time; meanwhile, the free painter will paint the walls at index 1 and 2, free of cost in 2 units of time. Thus, the total cost is 2 + 2 = 4.

Constraints: 1 ≤ cost.length ≤ 500 · cost.length == time.length · 1 ≤ cost[i] ≤ 10⁶ · 1 ≤ time[i] ≤ 500

Hint 1

While the paid painter works on wall i, how many walls can the free painter finish?

Hint 2

Think of each paid wall as covering 1 + time[i] walls: a knapsack.

From brute force to the pattern: Choosing subsets of paid walls is O(2ⁿ); the knapsack is O(n²).

Spot it: While the paid painter spends time[i] on a wall, the free painter can finish time[i] other walls. So choosing wall i for the paid painter "covers" 1 + time[i] walls at cost[i] → a 0/1 knapsack minimising cost to cover at least n walls.

Why not another pattern? Simulating schedules or trying subsets is exponential.

Approach:

  1. dp[c] = min cost to cover c walls (capped at n); dp[0] = 0.
  2. For each wall, for c from n down: dp[c] = min(dp[c], dp[max(0, c − 1 − time[i])] + cost[i]).
  3. Return dp[n].
class Solution:
    def paintWalls(self, cost: List[int], time: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(cost)
        INF = float("inf")
        dp = [0] + [INF] * n  # dp[c]: min cost so that c walls are taken care of
        for c_i, t_i in zip(cost, time):
            for c in range(n, 0, -1):  # 0/1 knapsack: go downwards
                dp[c] = min(dp[c], dp[max(0, c - 1 - t_i)] + c_i)  # this wall + t_i free ones
        return dp[n]
function paintWalls(cost: number[], time: number[]): number {
    const n = cost.length;
    const dp: number[] = [0, ...new Array(n).fill(Infinity)];  // dp[c]: min cost so that c walls are taken care of
    cost.forEach((ci, idx) => {
        const ti = time[idx];
        for (let c = n; c > 0; c--) {  // 0/1 knapsack: go downwards
            dp[c] = Math.min(dp[c], dp[Math.max(0, c - 1 - ti)] + ci);  // this wall + ti free ones
        }
    });
    return dp[n];
}
class Solution {
    public int paintWalls(int[] cost, int[] time) {
        int n = cost.length;
        int[] dp = new int[n + 1];  // dp[c]: min cost so that c walls are taken care of
        Arrays.fill(dp, Integer.MAX_VALUE / 2);  // "impossible", with room to add a cost
        dp[0] = 0;
        for (int idx = 0; idx < n; idx++) {
            int ci = cost[idx], ti = time[idx];
            for (int c = n; c > 0; c--) {  // 0/1 knapsack: go downwards
                dp[c] = Math.min(dp[c], dp[Math.max(0, c - 1 - ti)] + ci);  // this wall + ti free ones
            }
        }
        return dp[n];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Covering more than n walls is the same as covering n, hence the cap at 0 with max.
  2. The walls the free painter does are exactly the ones not chosen for the paid painter.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Long times (one paid wall covers everything).
  • All time 1.
  • Single wall.

Complexity: O(n²) time, O(n) space.

Hard 3130. Find All Possible Stable Binary Arrays II Amazon Array

Problem: Count binary arrays with exactly zero zeros and one ones where no run of equal bits is longer than limit (mod 10⁹ + 7).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: zero = 1, one = 1, limit = 2
Output: 2
Explanation: The two possible stable binary arrays are [1,0] and [0,1].
Example 2
Input: zero = 1, one = 2, limit = 1
Output: 1
Explanation: The only possible stable binary array is [1,0,1].

Constraints: 1 ≤ zero, one, limit ≤ 1000

Hint 1

DP over how many zeros and ones are used and what the last bit is.

Hint 2

Appending a bit is invalid only if it creates a run of length limit + 1. Count those cases and subtract.

From brute force to the pattern: Enumerating arrays is exponential; summing over run lengths is O(z · o · limit); the subtraction trick is O(z · o).

Spot it: Count arrays by (zeros used, ones used, last bit) → DP. Appending a 0 to any array is fine unless it creates a run of limit + 1 zeros; those bad cases are exactly the arrays that ended in 1 with i − limit − 1 zeros, so subtract them in O(1).

Why not another pattern? Summing over the last run length is O(zero · one · limit).

Approach:

  1. dp0[i][0] = 1 for 1 ≤ i ≤ limit; dp1[0][j] = 1 for 1 ≤ j ≤ limit.
  2. dp0[i][j] = dp0[i−1][j] + dp1[i−1][j] − dp1[i−limit−1][j] (last term when i > limit).
  3. dp1 symmetric; answer dp0 + dp1 at (zero, one).
class Solution:
    def numberOfStableArrays(self, zero: int, one: int, limit: int) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        dp0 = [[0] * (one + 1) for _ in range(zero + 1)]  # ends with 0
        dp1 = [[0] * (one + 1) for _ in range(zero + 1)]  # ends with 1
        for i in range(1, min(zero, limit) + 1):
            dp0[i][0] = 1  # a single run of zeros
        for j in range(1, min(one, limit) + 1):
            dp1[0][j] = 1
        for i in range(1, zero + 1):
            for j in range(1, one + 1):
                dp0[i][j] = dp0[i - 1][j] + dp1[i - 1][j]  # append a 0
                if i > limit:
                    dp0[i][j] -= dp1[i - limit - 1][j]  # that would make limit + 1 zeros in a row
                dp1[i][j] = dp0[i][j - 1] + dp1[i][j - 1]  # append a 1
                if j > limit:
                    dp1[i][j] -= dp0[i][j - limit - 1]
                dp0[i][j] %= MOD
                dp1[i][j] %= MOD
        return (dp0[zero][one] + dp1[zero][one]) % MOD
function numberOfStableArrays(zero: number, one: number, limit: number): number {
    const MOD = 1_000_000_007;
    const dp0: number[][] = Array.from({ length: zero + 1 }, () => new Array(one + 1).fill(0));  // ends with 0
    const dp1: number[][] = Array.from({ length: zero + 1 }, () => new Array(one + 1).fill(0));  // ends with 1
    for (let i = 1; i <= Math.min(zero, limit); i++) {
        dp0[i][0] = 1;  // a single run of zeros
    }
    for (let j = 1; j <= Math.min(one, limit); j++) {
        dp1[0][j] = 1;
    }
    for (let i = 1; i <= zero; i++) {
        for (let j = 1; j <= one; j++) {
            dp0[i][j] = dp0[i - 1][j] + dp1[i - 1][j];  // append a 0
            if (i > limit) {
                dp0[i][j] -= dp1[i - limit - 1][j];  // that would make limit + 1 zeros in a row
            }
            dp1[i][j] = dp0[i][j - 1] + dp1[i][j - 1];  // append a 1
            if (j > limit) {
                dp1[i][j] -= dp0[i][j - limit - 1];
            }
            dp0[i][j] = ((dp0[i][j] % MOD) + MOD) % MOD;  // + MOD: % can be negative here
            dp1[i][j] = ((dp1[i][j] % MOD) + MOD) % MOD;
        }
    }
    return (dp0[zero][one] + dp1[zero][one]) % MOD;
}
class Solution {
    public int numberOfStableArrays(int zero, int one, int limit) {
        final long MOD = 1_000_000_007;
        long[][] dp0 = new long[zero + 1][one + 1];  // ends with 0
        long[][] dp1 = new long[zero + 1][one + 1];  // ends with 1
        for (int i = 1; i <= Math.min(zero, limit); i++) {
            dp0[i][0] = 1;  // a single run of zeros
        }
        for (int j = 1; j <= Math.min(one, limit); j++) {
            dp1[0][j] = 1;
        }
        for (int i = 1; i <= zero; i++) {
            for (int j = 1; j <= one; j++) {
                dp0[i][j] = dp0[i - 1][j] + dp1[i - 1][j];  // append a 0
                if (i > limit) {
                    dp0[i][j] -= dp1[i - limit - 1][j];  // that would make limit + 1 zeros in a row
                }
                dp1[i][j] = dp0[i][j - 1] + dp1[i][j - 1];  // append a 1
                if (j > limit) {
                    dp1[i][j] -= dp0[i][j - limit - 1];
                }
                dp0[i][j] = (dp0[i][j] % MOD + MOD) % MOD;  // + MOD: % can be negative here
                dp1[i][j] = (dp1[i][j] % MOD + MOD) % MOD;
            }
        }
        return (int) ((dp0[zero][one] + dp1[zero][one]) % MOD);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Appending 0 to every valid array with i − 1 zeros counts all candidates; the only invalid ones end with exactly limit + 1 zeros.
  2. Those are a valid array ending in 1 with i − limit − 1 zeros, followed by limit + 1 zeros: dp1[i − limit − 1][j] of them.
  3. Python's % keeps values non-negative after the subtraction.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • limit ≥ zero and one (no restriction).
  • limit = 1 (strictly alternating).
  • One of the counts is 1.

Complexity: O(zero · one) time and space.

Hard 3995. Minimum Cost to Convert String III Amazon String

Problem: Rules pattern → replacement (with * wildcards) cost costs[i] + number of *. Each position can be rewritten at most once. Return the minimum cost to turn source into target, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: source = "hello", target = "world", rules = [["he","wo"],["llo","rld"]], costs = [3,4]
Output: 7
Explanation: Apply rules[0] to replace "he" with "wo" at cost 3, so the string becomes "wollo". Apply rules[1] to replace "llo" with "rld" at cost 4, so the string becomes "world". The total cost is 3 + 4 = 7.
Example 2
Input: source = "cat", target = "dog", rules = [["c*t","dog"]], costs = [2]
Output: 3
Explanation: Apply rules[0] to replace "cat" with "dog". The wildcard '*' matches 'a', adding 1 to the base cost 2. The total cost is 2 + 1 = 3.

Constraints: 1 ≤ source.length == target.length ≤ 5000 · source and target consist of lowercase English letters. · 1 ≤ rules.length == costs.length ≤ 200 · rules[i] = [patterni, replacementi] · 1 ≤ patterni.length == replacementi.length ≤ 20 · patterni contains at least one lowercase English letter and at most 5 '*' characters. · replacementi contains only lowercase English letters. · 1 ≤ costs[i] ≤ 1000

Hint 1

Since a position is used at most once, what does each rule application see and produce?

Hint 2

Split the string into untouched characters and rule blocks: DP over prefixes.

From brute force to the pattern: Searching rule sequences is exponential; prefix DP is polynomial.

Spot it: Because a position is never touched twice, every rule application acts on a block of the original source and must produce exactly the target there. So the string splits into untouched matching characters and rule blocks → DP over prefixes: dp[i] = cost to fix source[:i].

Why not another pattern? Searching sequences of rule applications is exponential.

Approach:

  1. dp[0] = 0.
  2. If source[i] == target[i], dp[i + 1] = min(dp[i + 1], dp[i]).
  3. For each rule of length L starting at i: pattern matches source[i:i+L] (with *) and replacement equals target[i:i+L] → dp[i + L] = min(dp[i + L], dp[i] + cost + stars).
class Solution:
    def minCost(self, source: str, target: str, rules: List[List[str]], costs: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(source)
        INF = float("inf")
        dp = [0] + [INF] * n  # dp[i]: cheapest way to make source[:i] equal target[:i]
        for i in range(n):
            if dp[i] == INF:
                continue
            if source[i] == target[i]:
                dp[i + 1] = min(dp[i + 1], dp[i])  # leave this character alone
            for (pattern, repl), cost in zip(rules, costs):
                L = len(pattern)
                if i + L > n or repl != target[i:i + L]:
                    continue  # must produce the target exactly
                if all(p == "*" or p == s for p, s in zip(pattern, source[i:i + L])):
                    dp[i + L] = min(dp[i + L], dp[i] + cost + pattern.count("*"))
        return dp[n] if dp[n] < INF else -1
function minCost(source: string, target: string, rules: string[][], costs: number[]): number {
    const n = source.length;
    const INF = Infinity;
    const dp: number[] = [0, ...new Array(n).fill(INF)];  // dp[i]: cheapest way to make source[:i] equal target[:i]
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (dp[i] === INF) {
            continue;
        }
        if (source[i] === target[i]) {
            dp[i + 1] = Math.min(dp[i + 1], dp[i]);  // leave this character alone
        }
        rules.forEach(([pattern, repl], r) => {
            const L = pattern.length;
            if (i + L > n || repl !== target.slice(i, i + L)) {
