                return;  // must produce the target exactly
            }
            if ([...pattern].every((p, t) => p === "*" || p === source[i + t])) {
                const stars = pattern.split("*").length - 1;
                dp[i + L] = Math.min(dp[i + L], dp[i] + costs[r] + stars);
            }
        });
    }
    return dp[n] < INF ? dp[n] : -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int minCost(String source, String target, List<List<String>> rules, int[] costs) {
        int n = source.length();
        final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE;
        long[] dp = new long[n + 1];  // dp[i]: cheapest way to make source[:i] equal target[:i]
        Arrays.fill(dp, INF);
        dp[0] = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (dp[i] == INF) {
                continue;
            }
            if (source.charAt(i) == target.charAt(i)) {
                dp[i + 1] = Math.min(dp[i + 1], dp[i]);  // leave this character alone
            }
            for (int r = 0; r < rules.size(); r++) {
                String pattern = rules.get(r).get(0), repl = rules.get(r).get(1);
                int L = pattern.length();
                if (i + L > n || !repl.equals(target.substring(i, i + L))) {
                    continue;  // must produce the target exactly
                }
                boolean fits = true;
                int stars = 0;
                for (int t = 0; t < L; t++) {
                    char p = pattern.charAt(t);
                    if (p == '*') {
                        stars++;
                    } else if (p != source.charAt(i + t)) {
                        fits = false;
                    }
                }
                if (fits) {
                    dp[i + L] = Math.min(dp[i + L], dp[i] + costs[r] + stars);
                }
            }
        }
        return dp[n] < INF ? (int) dp[n] : -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A rewritten block can't be changed again, so its replacement must already equal the target.
  2. Rule blocks never overlap and always match the original characters, so the DP over prefixes covers every valid plan.
  3. Wildcards match anything but add 1 each to the cost.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • source == target → 0.
  • No rule fits → −1.
  • Wildcards in patterns.

Complexity: O(n · Σ L) time over all rules, O(n) space.

Hard 2719. Count of Integers Cisco StringMath

Problem: Count integers in [num1, num2] (up to 10²²) whose digit sum is between min_sum and max_sum (mod 10⁹ + 7).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: num1 = "1", num2 = "12", min_sum = 1, max_sum = 8
Output: 11
Explanation: There are 11 integers whose sum of digits lies between 1 and 8 are 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,10,11, and 12. Thus, we return 11.
Example 2
Input: num1 = "1", num2 = "5", min_sum = 1, max_sum = 5
Output: 5
Explanation: The 5 integers whose sum of digits lies between 1 and 5 are 1,2,3,4, and 5. Thus, we return 5.

Constraints: 1 ≤ num1 ≤ num2 ≤ 10²² · 1 ≤ min_sum ≤ max_sum ≤ 400

Hint 1

Count up to a bound and subtract.

Hint 2

Build numbers digit by digit, tracking the digit sum and whether you're still on the bound.

From brute force to the pattern: Enumerating the range is impossible; the digit DP has about 20,000 states.

Spot it: Counting numbers up to a bound by a digit property → digit DP over (position, digit sum so far, tight).

Why not another pattern? Iterating up to 10²² numbers is impossible.

Approach:

  1. f(N) counts 0..N with digit sum in range: memoised go(pos, sum, tight).
  2. Answer f(num2) − f(num1) plus 1 if num1 itself qualifies.
from functools import lru_cache

class Solution:
    def count(self, num1: str, num2: str, min_sum: int, max_sum: int) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7

        def up_to(N):  # how many x in [0, N] have min_sum <= digit sum <= max_sum
            digits = list(map(int, N))

            @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
            def go(pos, total, tight):
                if total > max_sum:
                    return 0  # already too large
                if pos == len(digits):
                    return 1 if total >= min_sum else 0
                top = digits[pos] if tight else 9
                return sum(go(pos + 1, total + d, tight and d == top) for d in range(top + 1)) % MOD

            return go(0, 0, True)

        own = 1 if min_sum <= sum(map(int, num1)) <= max_sum else 0  # num1 itself
        return (up_to(num2) - up_to(num1) + own) % MOD
function count(num1: string, num2: string, min_sum: number, max_sum: number): number {
    const MOD = 1_000_000_007;

    const upTo = (N: string): number => {  // how many x in [0, N] have min_sum <= digit sum <= max_sum
        const digits = [...N].map(Number);
        const memo = new Map<string, number>();

        const go = (pos: number, total: number, tight: boolean): number => {
            if (total > max_sum) {
                return 0;  // already too large
            }
            if (pos === digits.length) {
                return total >= min_sum ? 1 : 0;
            }
            const key = `${pos},${total},${tight}`;
            if (memo.has(key)) {
                return memo.get(key)!;
            }
            const top = tight ? digits[pos] : 9;
            let sum = 0;
            for (let d = 0; d <= top; d++) {
                sum += go(pos + 1, total + d, tight && d === top);
            }
            memo.set(key, sum % MOD);
            return sum % MOD;
        };

        return go(0, 0, true);
    };

    const digitSum = [...num1].reduce((a, ch) => a + Number(ch), 0);
    const own = min_sum <= digitSum && digitSum <= max_sum ? 1 : 0;  // num1 itself
    return (((upTo(num2) - upTo(num1) + own) % MOD) + MOD) % MOD;
}
class Solution {
    private static final int MOD = 1_000_000_007;
    private int[] digits;
    private int minSum;
    private int maxSum;
    private Map<String, Integer> memo;

    public int count(String num1, String num2, int min_sum, int max_sum) {
        minSum = min_sum;
        maxSum = max_sum;
        int digitSum = 0;
        for (char ch : num1.toCharArray()) {
            digitSum += ch - '0';
        }
        int own = min_sum <= digitSum && digitSum <= max_sum ? 1 : 0;  // num1 itself
        long result = (long) upTo(num2) - upTo(num1) + own;
        return (int) ((result % MOD + MOD) % MOD);
    }

    // how many x in [0, N] have min_sum <= digit sum <= max_sum
    private int upTo(String N) {
        digits = new int[N.length()];
        for (int i = 0; i < digits.length; i++) {
            digits[i] = N.charAt(i) - '0';
        }
        memo = new HashMap<>();
        return go(0, 0, true);
    }

    private int go(int pos, int total, boolean tight) {
        if (total > maxSum) {
            return 0;  // already too large
        }
        if (pos == digits.length) {
            return total >= minSum ? 1 : 0;
        }
        String key = pos + "," + total + "," + tight;
        if (memo.containsKey(key)) {
            return memo.get(key);
        }
        int top = tight ? digits[pos] : 9;
        long sum = 0;
        for (int d = 0; d <= top; d++) {
            sum += go(pos + 1, total + d, tight && d == top);
        }
        int result = (int) (sum % MOD);
        memo.put(key, result);
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. tight means the prefix equals N's prefix, so the next digit is capped.
  2. Stopping when the sum exceeds max_sum prunes most states.
  3. f(num2) − f(num1) counts (num1, num2], so num1 is added back separately (avoids subtracting 1 from a string).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • num1 == num2.
  • num1 qualifies (added back).
  • max_sum larger than any digit sum.

Complexity: O(D · S · 10) time for D ≤ 23 digits and S ≤ 400.

Medium 464. Can I Win Microsoft Math

Problem: Players alternately take unused numbers 1..maxChoosableInteger; whoever makes the running total reach desiredTotal wins. Can the first player force a win?

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: maxChoosableInteger = 10, desiredTotal = 11
Output: false
Explanation: No matter which integer the first player choose, the first player will lose. The first player can choose an integer from 1 up to 10. If the first player choose 1, the second player can only choose integers from 2 up to 10. The second player will win by choosing 10 and get a total = 11, which is >= desiredTotal. Same with other integers chosen by the first player, the second player will always win.
Example 2
Input: maxChoosableInteger = 10, desiredTotal = 0
Output: true

Constraints: 1 ≤ maxChoosableInteger ≤ 20 · 0 ≤ desiredTotal ≤ 300

Hint 1

What fully describes a game position?

Hint 2

A position is winning if some move leads to a losing position for the opponent.

From brute force to the pattern: The game tree is m!; memoising on the used-set is O(2^m · m).

Spot it: The state is which numbers are used (the remaining total follows from it) → bitmask DP with memoisation, the classic win/lose game recursion.

Why not another pattern? Exploring the game tree without memo is factorial.

Approach:

  1. If the sum of all numbers < total, false; if total ≤ 0, true.
  2. win(mask, remaining): true if some unused x ≥ remaining, or some x with not win(mask | x, remaining − x).
from functools import lru_cache

class Solution:
    def canIWin(self, maxChoosableInteger: int, desiredTotal: int) -> bool:
        m = maxChoosableInteger
        if desiredTotal <= 0:
            return True
        if m * (m + 1) // 2 < desiredTotal:
            return False  # nobody can ever reach it

        @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
        def win(used, remaining):  # can the player to move force a win?
            for x in range(m, 0, -1):
                bit = 1 << x
                if used & bit:
                    continue
                if x >= remaining or not win(used | bit, remaining - x):
                    return True  # reach the total now, or leave a losing position
            return False

        return win(0, desiredTotal)
function canIWin(maxChoosableInteger: number, desiredTotal: number): boolean {
    const m = maxChoosableInteger;
    if (desiredTotal <= 0) {
        return true;
    }
    if ((m * (m + 1)) / 2 < desiredTotal) {
        return false;  // nobody can ever reach it
    }
    const memo = new Map<number, boolean>();  // the used set fixes what remains, so it is the whole key

    const win = (used: number, remaining: number): boolean => {  // can the player to move force a win?
        if (memo.has(used)) {
            return memo.get(used)!;
        }
        let result = false;
        for (let x = m; x > 0; x--) {
            const bit = 1 << x;
            if (used & bit) {
                continue;
            }
            if (x >= remaining || !win(used | bit, remaining - x)) {
                result = true;  // reach the total now, or leave a losing position
                break;
            }
        }
        memo.set(used, result);
        return result;
    };

    return win(0, desiredTotal);
}
class Solution {
    private int m;
    private Map<Integer, Boolean> memo;  // the used set fixes what remains, so it is the whole key

    public boolean canIWin(int maxChoosableInteger, int desiredTotal) {
        m = maxChoosableInteger;
        if (desiredTotal <= 0) {
            return true;
        }
        if (m * (m + 1) / 2 < desiredTotal) {
            return false;  // nobody can ever reach it
        }
        memo = new HashMap<>();
        return win(0, desiredTotal);
    }

    // can the player to move force a win?
    private boolean win(int used, int remaining) {
        if (memo.containsKey(used)) {
            return memo.get(used);
        }
        boolean result = false;
        for (int x = m; x > 0; x--) {
            int bit = 1 << x;
            if ((used & bit) != 0) {
                continue;
            }
            if (x >= remaining || !win(used | bit, remaining - x)) {
                result = true;  // reach the total now, or leave a losing position
                break;
            }
        }
        memo.put(used, result);
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. remaining is determined by used, so the cache size is bounded by 2^m.
  2. Trying big numbers first finds immediate wins sooner.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Total ≤ 0 → true.
  • Sum of all numbers too small → false.
  • First move wins immediately.

Complexity: O(2^m · m) time and space (m ≤ 20).

Medium 837. New 21 Game Microsoft Math

Problem: Starting at 0, draw uniform points 1..maxPts until reaching at least k. Return the probability of ending with at most n points.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 10, k = 1, maxPts = 10
Output: 1.00000
Explanation: Alice gets a single card, then stops.
Example 2
Input: n = 6, k = 1, maxPts = 10
Output: 0.60000
Explanation: Alice gets a single card, then stops. In 6 out of 10 possibilities, she is at or below 6 points.

Constraints: 0 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁴ · 1 ≤ maxPts ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

Write P[x] in terms of earlier P values.

Hint 2

That sum covers a fixed-size range: maintain it as a sliding window.

From brute force to the pattern: Summing maxPts terms per x is O(n · maxPts); the window is O(n).

Spot it: Probability DP: P[x] = (P[x − 1] + … + P[x − maxPts]) / maxPts, counting only previous totals below k (still drawing). The sum is a sliding window maintained in O(1).

Why not another pattern? Summing maxPts terms per state is O(n · maxPts).

Approach:

  1. If k == 0 or n ≥ k − 1 + maxPts, return 1.
  2. P[0] = 1, window = 1.
  3. For x = 1..n: P[x] = window / maxPts; add P[x] to the window if x < k; drop P[x − maxPts] if it was in the window.
  4. Answer: Σ P[k..n].
class Solution:
    def new21Game(self, n: int, k: int, maxPts: int) -> float:
        if k == 0 or n >= k - 1 + maxPts:
            return 1.0  # you can never exceed n
        P = [0.0] * (n + 1)
        P[0] = 1.0
        window = 1.0  # sum of P over the last maxPts totals that are still drawing (< k)
        for x in range(1, n + 1):
            P[x] = window / maxPts
            if x < k:
                window += P[x]  # x still draws again
            if x - maxPts >= 0 and x - maxPts < k:
                window -= P[x - maxPts]  # too far back to reach x + 1
        return sum(P[k:n + 1])
function new21Game(n: number, k: number, maxPts: number): number {
    if (k === 0 || n >= k - 1 + maxPts) {
        return 1.0;  // you can never exceed n
    }
    const P: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(0);
    P[0] = 1.0;
    let window = 1.0;  // sum of P over the last maxPts totals that are still drawing (< k)
    for (let x = 1; x <= n; x++) {
        P[x] = window / maxPts;
        if (x < k) {
            window += P[x];  // x still draws again
        }
        if (x - maxPts >= 0 && x - maxPts < k) {
            window -= P[x - maxPts];  // too far back to reach x + 1
        }
    }
    let total = 0;
    for (let x = k; x <= n; x++) {
        total += P[x];
    }
    return total;
}
class Solution {
    public double new21Game(int n, int k, int maxPts) {
        if (k == 0 || n >= k - 1 + maxPts) {
            return 1.0;  // you can never exceed n
        }
        double[] P = new double[n + 1];
        P[0] = 1.0;
        double window = 1.0;  // sum of P over the last maxPts totals that are still drawing (< k)
        for (int x = 1; x <= n; x++) {
            P[x] = window / maxPts;
            if (x < k) {
                window += P[x];  // x still draws again
            }
            if (x - maxPts >= 0 && x - maxPts < k) {
                window -= P[x - maxPts];  // too far back to reach x + 1
            }
        }
        double total = 0;
        for (int x = k; x <= n; x++) {
            total += P[x];
        }
        return total;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Only totals below k keep drawing, so only they feed later totals.
  2. The window slides by one each step: add the newest drawing total, drop the one too far back.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 0 → 1.
  • n large enough → 1.
  • maxPts = 1.

Complexity: O(n) time and space.

Medium 3946. Maximum Number of Items From Sale I Microsoft Array

Problem: Buying item i (any copies) also gives one free copy of every other item whose factor is a multiple of factor_i. Maximise the total copies within budget.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: items = [[6,2],[2,6],[3,4]], budget = 9
Output: 4
Explanation: You can buy 2 copies of item 0 and 1 copy of item 2 for a total cost of 2 * 2 + 4 = 8, which is not greater than budget = 9. Buying item 2 gives 1 free copy of item 0, because factor2 = 3 divides factor0 = 6. You leave with 3 purchased copies and 1 free copy, for a total of 4 item copies.
Example 2
Input: items = [[2,4],[3,2],[4,1],[6,4],[12,4]], budget = 8
Output: 10
Explanation: You can buy 1 copy of item 0, 1 copy of item 1, and 2 copies of item 2 for a total cost of 4 + 2 + 2 * 1 = 8. Buying item 0 gives 1 free copy of items 2, 3, and 4. Buying item 1 gives 1 free copy of items 3 and 4. Buying item 2 gives 1 free copy of item 4. Thus, you receive 6 free copies. You leave with 4 purchased copies and 6 free copies, for a total of 10 item copies.

Constraints: 1 ≤ items.length ≤ 1000 · items[i] = [factori, pricei] · 1 ≤ factori, pricei ≤ 1500 · 1 ≤ budget ≤ 1500

Hint 1

How much is the first copy of an item worth? How much is each additional copy worth?

Hint 2

Choose first copies with a knapsack; spend the rest on the cheapest item.

From brute force to the pattern: Subsets of item types are exponential; the knapsack is O(n · budget).

Spot it: Only the first copy of a type triggers its bonus: it's worth 1 + bonus_i at price_i. Extra copies are worth 1 each, so extras should be the cheapest item. That's a 0/1 knapsack on first copies plus leftover budget spent at the minimum price.

Why not another pattern? Greedy by value per price fails for knapsacks; trying all subsets is exponential.

Approach:

  1. bonus_i = number of j ≠ i with factor_i | factor_j.
  2. Knapsack dp[b] = best value of first copies costing exactly b.
  3. Answer: max(dp[b] + (budget − b) // min_price) over reachable b.
class Solution:
    def maximumSaleItems(self, items: List[List[int]], budget: int) -> int:
        n = len(items)
        bonus = [sum(1 for j in range(n) if j != i and items[j][0] % items[i][0] == 0) for i in range(n)]
        NEG = float("-inf")
        dp = [0] + [NEG] * budget  # dp[b]: best value from first copies costing exactly b
        for (factor, price), extra in zip(items, bonus):
            value = 1 + extra  # the copy itself plus its free copies
            for b in range(budget, price - 1, -1):  # 0/1: each type's first copy once
                if dp[b - price] + value > dp[b]:
                    dp[b] = dp[b - price] + value
        cheapest = min(price for _, price in items)
        return max(dp[b] + (budget - b) // cheapest for b in range(budget + 1) if dp[b] != NEG)  # extra copies at the lowest price
function maximumSaleItems(items: number[][], budget: number): number {
    const n = items.length;
    const bonus = items.map(([fi], i) => items.filter(([fj], j) => j !== i && fj % fi === 0).length);
    const NEG = -Infinity;
    const dp: number[] = [0, ...new Array(budget).fill(NEG)];  // dp[b]: best value from first copies costing exactly b
    items.forEach(([, price], i) => {
        const value = 1 + bonus[i];  // the copy itself plus its free copies
        for (let b = budget; b >= price; b--) {  // 0/1: each type's first copy once
            if (dp[b - price] + value > dp[b]) {
                dp[b] = dp[b - price] + value;
            }
        }
    });
    const cheapest = Math.min(...items.map(([, price]) => price));
    let best = NEG;
    for (let b = 0; b <= budget; b++) {
        if (dp[b] !== NEG) {
            best = Math.max(best, dp[b] + Math.floor((budget - b) / cheapest));  // extra copies at the lowest price
        }
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int maximumSaleItems(int[][] items, int budget) {
        int n = items.length;
        int[] bonus = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                if (j != i && items[j][0] % items[i][0] == 0) {
                    bonus[i]++;
                }
            }
        }
        final int NEG = Integer.MIN_VALUE;  // "no way to spend exactly b"; never added to
        int[] dp = new int[budget + 1];  // dp[b]: best value from first copies costing exactly b
        Arrays.fill(dp, NEG);
        dp[0] = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int price = items[i][1];
            int value = 1 + bonus[i];  // the copy itself plus its free copies
            for (int b = budget; b >= price; b--) {  // 0/1: each type's first copy once
                if (dp[b - price] != NEG && dp[b - price] + value > dp[b]) {
                    dp[b] = dp[b - price] + value;
                }
            }
        }
        int cheapest = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int[] item : items) {
            cheapest = Math.min(cheapest, item[1]);
        }
        int best = NEG;
        for (int b = 0; b <= budget; b++) {
            if (dp[b] != NEG) {
                best = Math.max(best, dp[b] + (budget - b) / cheapest);  // extra copies at the lowest price
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Free copies depend only on which types are bought, not how many copies.
  2. Any additional purchased copy is worth exactly 1, so the cheapest item is the best extra (whether or not it was a first copy).
  3. Using exact-cost knapsack states lets the leftover be computed precisely.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Budget below every price → 0.
  • Factor 1 (gives a copy of everything).
  • Duplicate factors.

Complexity: O(n² + n · budget) time, O(budget) space.

Hard 2472. Maximum Number of Non-overlapping Palindrome Substrings Microsoft String

Problem: Select the most non-overlapping palindromic substrings, each of length at least k.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "abaccdbbd", k = 3
Output: 2
Explanation: We can select the substrings underlined in s = "abaccdbbd". Both "aba" and "dbbd" are palindromes and have a length of at least k = 3. It can be shown that we cannot find a selection with more than two valid substrings.
Example 2
Input: s = "adbcda", k = 2
Output: 0
Explanation: There is no palindrome substring of length at least 2 in the string.

Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ s.length ≤ 2000 · s consists of lowercase English letters.

Hint 1

Use a prefix DP over the string.

Hint 2

Do you ever need a palindrome longer than k + 1?

From brute force to the pattern: All palindromic substrings with an interval DP is O(n²); restricting to lengths k, k + 1 gives O(nk).

Spot it: Prefix DP: dp[i] = best for s[:i]. Any palindrome of length ≥ k + 2 contains a shorter one (strip both ends) that is also long enough, so only lengths k and k + 1 ending at i need checking.

Why not another pattern? Checking all palindromic substrings is O(n²) states with O(n) checks.

Approach:

  1. dp[0] = 0; dp[i] = dp[i − 1] (skip a character).
  2. If s[i−k:i] is a palindrome: dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[i − k] + 1); same for length k + 1.
class Solution:
    def maxPalindromes(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        dp = [0] * (n + 1)  # dp[i]: most palindromes in s[:i]

        def is_pal(a, b):
            return s[a:b] == s[a:b][::-1]

        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            dp[i] = dp[i - 1]  # character i-1 unused
            for L in (k, k + 1):  # shortest qualifying palindromes are enough
                if i - L >= 0 and is_pal(i - L, i):
                    dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[i - L] + 1)
        return dp[n]
function maxPalindromes(s: string, k: number): number {
    const n = s.length;
    const dp: number[] = new Array(n + 1).fill(0);  // dp[i]: most palindromes in s.slice(0, i)

    const isPal = (a: number, b: number): boolean => {
        const piece = s.slice(a, b);
        return piece === [...piece].reverse().join("");
    };

    for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1];  // character i-1 unused
        for (const L of [k, k + 1]) {  // shortest qualifying palindromes are enough
            if (i - L >= 0 && isPal(i - L, i)) {
                dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[i - L] + 1);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[n];
}
class Solution {
    public int maxPalindromes(String s, int k) {
        int n = s.length();
        int[] dp = new int[n + 1];  // dp[i]: most palindromes in s.substring(0, i)
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            dp[i] = dp[i - 1];  // character i-1 unused
            for (int L = k; L <= k + 1; L++) {  // shortest qualifying palindromes are enough
                if (i - L >= 0 && isPal(s, i - L, i)) {
                    dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[i - L] + 1);
                }
            }
        }
        return dp[n];
    }

    private boolean isPal(String s, int a, int b) {
        String piece = s.substring(a, b);
        return piece.equals(new StringBuilder(piece).reverse().toString());
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Replacing a long palindrome by the shorter one in its middle frees characters and keeps the count.
  2. The middle of a palindrome of length L ≥ k + 2 has length L − 2 ≥ k.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 1 (every character).
  • No palindrome long enough → 0.
  • Overlapping candidates.

Complexity: O(n · k) time, O(n) space.

Hard 2977. Minimum Cost to Convert String II Microsoft StringGraph

Problem: Rules convert a substring x to y at a cost (repeatable on the same block, blocks otherwise disjoint). Return the minimum cost to turn source into target, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: source = "abcd", target = "acbe", original = ["a","b","c","c","e","d"], changed = ["b","c","b","e","b","e"], cost = [2,5,5,1,2,20]
Output: 28
Explanation: To convert "abcd" to "acbe", do the following operations: - Change substring source[1..1] from "b" to "c" at a cost of 5. - Change substring source[2..2] from "c" to "e" at a cost of 1. - Change substring source[2..2] from "e" to "b" at a cost of 2. - Change substring source[3..3] from "d" to "e" at a cost of 20. The total cost incurred is 5 + 1 + 2 + 20 = 28. It can be shown that this is the minimum possible cost.
Example 2
Input: source = "abcdefgh", target = "acdeeghh", original = ["bcd","fgh","thh"], changed = ["cde","thh","ghh"], cost = [1,3,5]
Output: 9
Explanation: To convert "abcdefgh" to "acdeeghh", do the following operations: - Change substring source[1..3] from "bcd" to "cde" at a cost of 1. - Change substring source[5..7] from "fgh" to "thh" at a cost of 3. We can do this operation because indices [5,7] are disjoint with indices picked in the first operation. - Change substring source[5..7] from "thh" to "ghh" at a cost of 5. We can do this operation because indices [5,7] are disjoint with indices picked in the first operation, and identical with indices picked in the second operation. The total cost incurred is 1 + 3 + 5 = 9. It can be shown that this is the minimum possible cost.

Constraints: 1 ≤ source.length == target.length ≤ 1000 · source, target consist only of lowercase English characters. · 1 ≤ cost.length == original.length == changed.length ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ original[i].length == changed[i].length ≤ source.length · original[i], changed[i] consist only of lowercase English characters. · original[i] != changed[i] · 1 ≤ cost[i] ≤ 10⁶

Hint 1

Converting the same block several times is a shortest path between strings.

Hint 2

Different blocks are disjoint: use a DP over prefixes.

From brute force to the pattern: Searching sequences of operations is exponential; Floyd + prefix DP is polynomial.

Spot it: Two layers: repeated conversions of one block form a shortest path between strings → Floyd–Warshall over the distinct rule strings. Then blocks are disjoint → a prefix DP: dp[i + L] = dp[i] + dist(source[i:i+L], target[i:i+L]) for every rule length L.

Why not another pattern? Trying conversion sequences is exponential.

Approach:

  1. Give each distinct string an id; dist[a][b] = min rule cost; Floyd–Warshall (only same-length strings connect).
  2. dp[0] = 0; if source[i] == target[i], dp[i + 1] = dp[i].
  3. For each rule length L: if both slices have ids and dist is finite, dp[i + L] = min(dp[i + L], dp[i] + dist).
class Solution:
    def minimumCost(self, source: str, target: str, original: List[str], changed: List[str], cost: List[int]) -> int:
        ids = {}
        for w in original + changed:
            ids.setdefault(w, len(ids))
        m = len(ids)
        INF = float("inf")
        dist = [[INF] * m for _ in range(m)]
        for i in range(m):
            dist[i][i] = 0
        for a, b, c in zip(original, changed, cost):
            dist[ids[a]][ids[b]] = min(dist[ids[a]][ids[b]], c)
        for mid in range(m):  # Floyd-Warshall: chains of conversions on one block
            dm = dist[mid]
            for i in range(m):
                dim = dist[i][mid]
                if dim == INF:
                    continue
                di = dist[i]
                for j in range(m):
                    if dim + dm[j] < di[j]:
                        di[j] = dim + dm[j]
        lengths = sorted({len(w) for w in original})
        n = len(source)
        dp = [0] + [INF] * n  # dp[i]: cheapest way to fix source[:i]
        for i in range(n):
            if dp[i] == INF:
                continue
            if source[i] == target[i]:
                dp[i + 1] = min(dp[i + 1], dp[i])  # nothing to convert here
            for L in lengths:
                if i + L > n:
                    break
                a, b = ids.get(source[i:i + L]), ids.get(target[i:i + L])
                if a is not None and b is not None and dist[a][b] < INF:
                    dp[i + L] = min(dp[i + L], dp[i] + dist[a][b])  # convert this whole block
        return dp[n] if dp[n] < INF else -1
function minimumCost(source: string, target: string, original: string[], changed: string[], cost: number[]): number {
    const ids = new Map<string, number>();
    for (const w of [...original, ...changed]) {
        if (!ids.has(w)) {
            ids.set(w, ids.size);
        }
    }
    const m = ids.size;
    const INF = Infinity;
    const dist: number[][] = Array.from({ length: m }, () => new Array(m).fill(INF));
    for (let i = 0; i < m; i++) {
        dist[i][i] = 0;
    }
    original.forEach((a, t) => {
        const ia = ids.get(a)!, ib = ids.get(changed[t])!;
        dist[ia][ib] = Math.min(dist[ia][ib], cost[t]);
    });
    for (let mid = 0; mid < m; mid++) {  // Floyd-Warshall: chains of conversions on one block
        const dm = dist[mid];
        for (let i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            const dim = dist[i][mid];
            if (dim === INF) {
                continue;
            }
            const di = dist[i];
            for (let j = 0; j < m; j++) {
                if (dim + dm[j] < di[j]) {
                    di[j] = dim + dm[j];
                }
            }
        }
    }
    const lengths = [...new Set(original.map((w) => w.length))].sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const n = source.length;
    const dp: number[] = [0, ...new Array(n).fill(INF)];  // dp[i]: cheapest way to fix source[:i]
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (dp[i] === INF) {
            continue;
        }
        if (source[i] === target[i]) {
            dp[i + 1] = Math.min(dp[i + 1], dp[i]);  // nothing to convert here
        }
        for (const L of lengths) {
            if (i + L > n) {
                break;
            }
            const a = ids.get(source.slice(i, i + L)), b = ids.get(target.slice(i, i + L));
            if (a !== undefined && b !== undefined && dist[a][b] < INF) {
                dp[i + L] = Math.min(dp[i + L], dp[i] + dist[a][b]);  // convert this whole block
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[n] < INF ? dp[n] : -1;
}
class Solution {
    public long minimumCost(String source, String target, String[] original, String[] changed, int[] cost) {
        Map<String, Integer> ids = new HashMap<>();
        for (String w : original) {
            ids.putIfAbsent(w, ids.size());
        }
        for (String w : changed) {
            ids.putIfAbsent(w, ids.size());
        }
        int m = ids.size();
        final long INF = Long.MAX_VALUE / 4;  // "no conversion", with room to add two of them
        long[][] dist = new long[m][m];
        for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
            Arrays.fill(dist[i], INF);
            dist[i][i] = 0;
        }
        for (int t = 0; t < original.length; t++) {
            int ia = ids.get(original[t]), ib = ids.get(changed[t]);
            dist[ia][ib] = Math.min(dist[ia][ib], cost[t]);
        }
        for (int mid = 0; mid < m; mid++) {  // Floyd-Warshall: chains of conversions on one block
            long[] dm = dist[mid];
            for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) {
                long dim = dist[i][mid];
                if (dim == INF) {
                    continue;
                }
                long[] di = dist[i];
                for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) {
                    if (dim + dm[j] < di[j]) {
                        di[j] = dim + dm[j];
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        TreeSet<Integer> lengths = new TreeSet<>();
        for (String w : original) {
            lengths.add(w.length());
        }
        int n = source.length();
        long[] dp = new long[n + 1];  // dp[i]: cheapest way to fix source[:i]
        Arrays.fill(dp, INF);
        dp[0] = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (dp[i] == INF) {
                continue;
            }
            if (source.charAt(i) == target.charAt(i)) {
                dp[i + 1] = Math.min(dp[i + 1], dp[i]);  // nothing to convert here
            }
            for (int L : lengths) {
                if (i + L > n) {
                    break;
                }
                Integer a = ids.get(source.substring(i, i + L)), b = ids.get(target.substring(i, i + L));
                if (a != null && b != null && dist[a][b] < INF) {
                    dp[i + L] = Math.min(dp[i + L], dp[i] + dist[a][b]);  // convert this whole block
                }
            }
        }
        return dp[n] < INF ? dp[n] : -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Operations on the same block can chain (x → y → z), which is a path in the graph of strings; Floyd–Warshall gives all cheapest chains.
  2. Different blocks never overlap, so the string splits into converted blocks and untouched equal characters: the prefix DP.
  3. Only rule lengths can form a converted block.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Impossible → −1.
  • Chained conversions on one block.
  • Equal substrings need no cost.

Complexity: O(m³ + n · R · L) for m ≤ 200 distinct strings, R distinct lengths and slice length L.

Medium 688. Knight Probability in Chessboard Apple Matrix

Problem: A knight makes k random moves (each of 8 directions equally likely). Return the probability it is still on the board.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 3, k = 2, row = 0, column = 0
Output: 0.06250
Explanation: There are two moves (to (1,2), (2,1)) that will keep the knight on the board. From each of those positions, there are also two moves that will keep the knight on the board. The total probability the knight stays on the board is 0.0625.
Example 2
Input: n = 1, k = 0, row = 0, column = 0
Output: 1.00000

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 25 · 0 ≤ k ≤ 100 · 0 ≤ row, column ≤ n - 1

Hint 1

Track the probability of being on each cell after each move.

Hint 2

Each cell distributes 1/8 of its probability to each knight target.

From brute force to the pattern: All 8ᵏ sequences vs O(k n²) DP.

Spot it: Probabilities after t moves depend only on those after t − 1 → DP over moves on an n × n grid: each cell sends 1/8 of its probability to every target that stays on the board (mass that falls off is lost).

Why not another pattern? Simulating all 8ᵏ move sequences is impossible for k = 100.

Approach:

  1. prob[row][column] = 1.
  2. Repeat k times: new grid, each cell spreads p / 8 to its on-board knight targets.
  3. Return the sum of the final grid.
class Solution:
    def knightProbability(self, n: int, k: int, row: int, column: int) -> float:
        moves = [(1, 2), (2, 1), (2, -1), (1, -2), (-1, -2), (-2, -1), (-2, 1), (-1, 2)]
        prob = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        prob[row][column] = 1.0
        for _ in range(k):
            nxt = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
            for r in range(n):
                for c in range(n):
                    p = prob[r][c]
                    if p:
                        for dr, dc in moves:
                            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                            if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n:
                                nxt[nr][nc] += p / 8  # moves off the board are simply lost
            prob = nxt
        return sum(map(sum, prob))
function knightProbability(n: number, k: number, row: number, column: number): number {
    const moves = [[1, 2], [2, 1], [2, -1], [1, -2], [-1, -2], [-2, -1], [-2, 1], [-1, 2]];
    let prob: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0));
    prob[row][column] = 1.0;
    for (let step = 0; step < k; step++) {
        const nxt: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(0));
        for (let r = 0; r < n; r++) {
            for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                const p = prob[r][c];
                if (p) {
                    for (const [dr, dc] of moves) {
                        const nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
                        if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n) {
                            nxt[nr][nc] += p / 8;  // moves off the board are simply lost
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        prob = nxt;
    }
    // add each row first, then the row totals (the same order as summing row by row)
    return prob.map((r) => r.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
class Solution {
    public double knightProbability(int n, int k, int row, int column) {
        int[][] moves = {{1, 2}, {2, 1}, {2, -1}, {1, -2}, {-1, -2}, {-2, -1}, {-2, 1}, {-1, 2}};
        double[][] prob = new double[n][n];
        prob[row][column] = 1.0;
        for (int step = 0; step < k; step++) {
            double[][] nxt = new double[n][n];
            for (int r = 0; r < n; r++) {
                for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                    double p = prob[r][c];
                    if (p != 0) {
                        for (int[] mv : moves) {
                            int nr = r + mv[0], nc = c + mv[1];
                            if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n) {
                                nxt[nr][nc] += p / 8;  // moves off the board are simply lost
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            prob = nxt;
        }
        // add each row first, then the row totals (the same order as summing row by row)
        double total = 0;
        for (double[] r : prob) {
            double rowSum = 0;
            for (double v : r) {
                rowSum += v;
            }
            total += rowSum;
        }
        return total;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each move multiplies by 1/8 per direction; probability leaving the board never returns.
  2. The total remaining mass is the probability of staying on.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 0 → 1.
  • n = 1 → 0 for k > 0.
  • Starting in a corner.

Complexity: O(k · n² · 8) time, O(n²) space.
